en: Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra,
First Chapter of the Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra.
Filled with the Uḍḍīśa [tantra] and crowded with throngs of yogis,
the goddess Gaurī, bowing her head, questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, O Protector of the World, O Sovereign of the Universe, I wish to hear [this]."
"O Lord of Gods, show favor and speak that which accomplishes the goals of dharma and artha.
[Tell us of] subjugation, eradication, delusion, and likewise immobilization;
as well as pacification, nourishment, and many other such rites."
O Maheśāna, [there are] the loss of sight, and likewise the loss of hearing;
the loss of knowledge, the loss of action, and furthermore the *kīlaka* (stake);
O Sureśāna, the paralysis of activity, as well as drying up and filling.
O Lord, tell me all of that, especially regarding the meditation on mantras;
and furthermore, O Bhairava, by your grace, speak of other various rites,
through the mere knowledge of which a person becomes rare on this earth.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O lady of excellent hips, for if you ask for the sake of spiritual perfection, I shall tell it to you, O Goddess; all that has been fully declared.
One shall slay the enemy by means of medicinal herbs and the recitation of mantras; of this there is no doubt.
Having extracted the essence from the Uḍḍīśa, I have spoken this to you out of devotion.
And having paid homage to the Uḍḍīśa and to Rudra, who is indeed very difficult to attain.
I shall describe the yogas arising from Rudra— the matted-haired, the odd-eyed, who removes the fear of all beings— which destroy all enemies;
when these are employed, he kills their vital breaths, without a doubt.
The first is the act of bringing beings under one's power, the second is intoxication,
the third is inciting hatred, and the fourth is likewise expulsion;
the fifth is the expulsion of a village, and the sixth is the freezing of water.
Furthermore, [I shall teach] the method for the immobilization of fire and the supreme means of subjugation.
O fair-faced one, hear also of many other applications—
the yogas taught by Śiva in the *Uḍḍīśa*, the definitive scripture.
It causes blindness, muteness, and deafness;
it brings about elemental fever and the neutralization of missiles and weapons;
it pacifies defects in water and destroys the potency of curd and honey.
It causes destruction and madness, and provokes elephants and horses;
it certainly effects the attraction of serpents as well as of men,
and it brings about the extinguishing of fire and the withering of leaves.
The transformation of oneself into a donkey, entering another's body,
the accomplishment of a *vetāla* or magical sandals, as well as fire emerging from the womb,
and many other fierce practices that cause the hair to stand on end.
The applications of spells and mantras, as well as the medicinal herbs used for malevolent rites—
whether they be secret or more deeply concealed— must be kept hidden and guarded with great effort.
What can one who does not know the Uḍḍīśa do, even if he is enraged?
One might move Mount Sumeru from its place, flood the earth with oceans, or cause the sun to fall to the ground; yet this [word of mine] shall not prove false.
Just as is the thunderbolt of Indra and the noose of Varuṇa, so too is my word.
Just as Yama’s staff, Kubera’s mace,
the spear of Agni as it is described, the sword of Nirṛti, the goad of Vāyu, and the trident of the wielder of the spear; UT_1.21–22.
Just as Skanda possesses his spear and Viṣṇu his Sudarśana discus,
so too these great yogas are employed for the sake of the enemy; they do not fail until their purpose is achieved, for they are unfailing— of this there is no doubt.
For one who is content and diligent, success comes through thorough reflection.
I shall describe the supreme ritual for subduing enemies, which,
as soon as it is performed, causes a spirit to seize a human being.
Taking a piece of nimba wood measuring four finger-breadths in length,
and having smeared it with the excrement of an enemy, one should likewise write the name [of that enemy].
O Maheśvarī, one should offer incense with the charcoal from a funeral pyre while uttering that name.
Having stationed oneself at the edge of a funeral pyre, one should take earth from the body of a corpse on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
if consecrated with this mantra, a spirit will quickly seize that [earth]. (UT 1.27–1.28)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of all beings, Virūpākṣa, who is eternally fierce, fanged, and terrifying;
together with the planets, yakṣas, bhūtas, and vetālas, O Śaṅkara, burn, burn, cook, cook, seize, seize, cause to be seized, cause to be seized the human being!
Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
If one desires to bring [the deity] back, this rite is performed for that purpose:
one should cause the Lord Īśāna to be gratified with ghee and *vacā* root;
one should offer incense of *guggulu* mixed with ghee on all sides.
Having consecrated [the patient] with the mantra, it is said that health will then be restored.
The mantra is: *Oṃ namaḥ śivāya śāntāya prabhāya muktāya devādhidevāya śubhrabāhave vyādhiṃ śamaya śamaya; may so-and-so become healthy; obeisance be to you!* This is the mantra for health.
Now I shall explain another practice that is difficult to find on earth,
by the mere performance of which fever seizes a human being.
Having fashioned a figure out of neem wood measuring four finger-breadths in size, [one should proceed].
Having written her name upon its heart with poison, *viṣonmatta* seeds, and salt,
and then having placed it in the raw hide while it is being cooked,
one should thereafter recite the mantra one hundred and eight times using the name of the enemy.
Then, within half a watch (prahara), he is seized by the fever-spirit.

Now follows the mantra for recitation: *Oṃ bakāmukhā Cāmuṇḍā, you who consume the milk, flesh, and blood of [Name], seize [Name] with fever! KHAḤ KHAḤ! Seize, seize! Cause to be seized, cause to be seized! HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!* If one desires to bring [the victim] back, this ritual procedure is performed for that purpose. UT 1.34.
When the syllables of the name of one who has bathed in milk are [recited], then he shall become healthy.
Now I shall further explain another practice, difficult to find on earth,
by the mere knowledge of which the eradication of an enemy occurs.
Having taken *brahmadaṇḍī*, funeral ashes, and likewise cow dung,
as well as alkali combined with *kākajaṅghā*,
one should throw it upon the heads of enemies; thus one will swiftly cause the foe to be eradicated.
Then one should bathe him with cow's milk;
thereafter, by shaving the hair, he will certainly become healthy.
Now I shall further explain another excellent method for the eradication of an enemy.
The incense named Nirbhedaka was spoken by Rudra himself:
the *brahmadaṇḍī* plant together with its roots, combined with *kākajaṅghā* and the sloughed skin of the king of serpents— this incense shall cause enemies to be eradicated.

Taking the slough of a snake and likewise the head of a black cobra, one should bury them at the door of whichever person [one intends]; that person is forcibly expelled. [Likewise,] *brahmadaṇḍī*, *surāmāṃsī*, and the head of a tortoise...
One should place [the substance] mixed with cremation-ground ashes into a human skull;
by burying it at the gate of the enemy, one quickly causes the foes to be driven away.
O Goddess of Gods, within seven nights, the house perishes along with its very roots.
Now I shall describe the rite of inciting enmity against enemies; listen, O Śaṅkarī, by the mere performance of which hatred arises among men.
The *brahmadaṇḍī* plant, together with its roots, combined with the flesh of a crow—
It should be infused repeatedly with the juices of *jātī* flowers for seven nights;
thereafter, one should infuse it with cat urine for seven days.
This incense should then be offered in the midst of the enemy's clan.
Just as a father smells the scent [of conflict] when there is strife with his sons,
so too is there supreme hostility between them and their friends and kinsmen.
It is declared that restoration to health is achieved through the incense of ghee and guggulu.
Now, regarding the rite of killing:
the wise practitioner, having taken liquor and human flesh,
as well as vulture bone and the excrement of an enemy, should bury them in the middle of the doorway.
Within seven days, one becomes Māra, as spoken by Rudra:
[the powder of] *brahmadaṇḍī*, funeral ashes, combined with wine, meat, the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, poison, and blood. (UT 1.49–1.50)
And it should be employed for the delusion of enemies through the application of the *nāma* [mantra];
by its application for seven nights, there is the destruction of all enemies.
This has been declared as that [application] for the enemy regarding these wicked yogas.
Having consecrated [the substance] one hundred and eight times with the mantra, the wise practitioner,

having fasted for one night and being composed in mind on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, should recite: *Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīuḍḍāmareśvarāya amukam uccāṭaya uccāṭaya vidveṣaya vidveṣaya svāhā*.

Having worshipped the god Īśāna, one should recite this mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of accomplishment, desiring success. It should be employed against an enemy army by a king seeking victory.
The tail of a house lizard, the head of a chameleon,
combined with an *indragopaka* insect, and likewise the head of a jackal—
these should be made into fine powders in equal proportions.
Indeed, when not yet liberated, one must employ everything; it shall take away the lives of a hundred people.
Human skull, urine, the head of an owl, the tail of a scorpion, and even *hālāhala* poison—UT_1.57.
Having taken equal parts of white frog meat and the urine of both an elephant and a camel, one should have them made into a fine powder; then,
having dried these, one should repeatedly prepare a paste (kalka).
Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to Yama, the destroyer of enemies!
This [mantra] should be offered with food and drink; it destroys the enemy army.
By the mere touch of that [substance], eruptions break out on all sides.
In his body there shall arise a violent fever and intense pain;
he will die within seven nights unless he is brought back [to life].
Now I shall explain another method for the accomplishment of which meditation is the means.
And this was indeed declared by Rudra out of grace to the thirty gods:
the blood of a black snake, of a certain cock, of a tortoise, and of peacocks; as well as rocanā and genuine añjana.
Saffron, bhadramusta, tagara, and black [tagara]—
one should collect these in equal parts under the asterism Puṣya on a Sunday. Having ground them under the asterism Aśleṣā, one should place them in a silver vessel.
One should place it on the ground for ten days; afterwards, having lifted it up, one should smear it.
This is called the *Asidhārāṅgadā*, spoken by Rudra himself.
Then, one should smear the limbs, or even the bones.
Likewise, upon fruits, flowers, leaves, and similarly with the finest incenses—
this great mantra is a panacea that strikes fear into malevolent spirits.
Having consecrated food and drink with it, one should employ them according to the prescribed rite.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to Rudra, the peaceful one, possessed of divine yoga and divine form, the matted-haired celibate student, the one consecrated by the gods and possessing a hundred great powers; *manohaṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*.
Having become pure and composed, one who is being afflicted should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times. UT 1.68.
And with a young girl, one should diligently grind [the substance] in the middle of a cow-pen;
if that is impossible, then on a funeral pyre, again and again according to one's ability.
This was proclaimed by Rudra himself as the accomplisher of all undertakings.

All [mantras] indeed should be employed, for they are the destroyers of all enemies. Therefore, one who is skilled in application should protect them with every effort; however, it is not taught that they should be used when one has not eaten, nor toward a cruel person or a sinful individual.
"It should be given to one who is endowed with devotion and knowledgeable in the scriptures, O Goddess of the Immortals.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Uḍḍāmareśvara-mahātantra*, extracted from the *Vīrabhadreśvara-tantra* in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva.
*Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra*, 1.72.
The Second Chapter.
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for paralyzing water:
[the blood and flesh] of the crocodile, the *velva*, and the *daṃṣṭra* [creature]. (UT 2.1)
One should repeatedly place the heart of a tortoise and that of a porpoise together with the oil of the *vibhītaka* tree;
having performed the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one may then remain in the water as one pleases.
The juice of *madraka*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *makara* should be taken;
the head of a *ḍuṇḍubha* should be taken, and all these should be combined together.
They should be administered while oil of *vibhītaka* is being cooked.
One should perform the rite of deposition (*nyāsa*); the oil remains in the water for seven days.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, being composed, one should cook that oil in an iron vessel.
Having fasted for four months and worshipped the god Śaṅkara, [one should proceed].
Having consecrated the clay for the ritual bath with the mantra one thousand and eight times, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
By consecrating it with this mantra, success is achieved; not otherwise.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara! Paralyze the water, paralyze it! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Now I shall explain the preparation of the spider-poison; listen to that in brief.
[It consists of] the juice of *bhallātaka*, *guñjā*, poison, and *citraka*.
One should administer the powder of *kapikacchū* hair;
this, combined with all [the aforementioned ingredients], is the supreme method for producing a spider-bite (*lūtā*).
I shall now describe its appearance, by which characteristics it arises.
The limbs become covered in smoke and repeatedly faint;
such would be the form of its symptoms when afflicted by a spider.
I shall describe its treatment, by which one attains well-being.
Uśīra, sandalwood, priyaṅgu, tagara, red sandalwood, and kuṣṭha—this ointment destroys spiders. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara; to the one who causes trembling, svāhā!
Having consecrated it with mantras, he will then become healthy.
One should take the head of a black cobra, place mustard seeds in its mouth,
combine them with *bhallātaka* fruit, and wrap it with a black thread.
One should cook it with smoke inside a hollow of anthill clay.
Having mixed the powder of the poison with a sixteenth part of the hair of a *kapikacchapa*,
one should cast it upon the heads of enemies.
The application of spiders is most excellent during the autumn, summer, and spring.
When the body has been fomented, mustard seeds adhere to it;
one should then cause a venomous spider to attach itself—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
By the mere arising of the sensation, the mantra recitation is performed as before;
by the previous procedure, one becomes restored as before.
Now, I shall briefly describe the destruction of crops.

As soon as it has been performed, the wise one, having fashioned a vajra, should cast it upon whichever field he desires; therein occurs the destruction of the crops. The knower of mantras should cast it there by means of the Māhendra application.
Now I shall again declare the mantra to be employed in the ritual applications:
one should consecrate [the object] with this mantra one hundred and eight times:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya vajraṃ vināśaya vajraṃ surapatir ājñāpayati huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One who applies this yoga through ritual action according to the prescribed method, by means of the application of leaves, shall cause a leaf to perish as it is cast away.
Furthermore, I shall describe the rite of eradication; listen, my son, exactly as it is.
By the mere performance of which, the expulsion of a village occurs.
Having taken earth from the four crossroads of the village, the wise one should fashion an image with cow dung from the four directions of the village.
Having prepared the fire from the wood of the funeral pyre with the feathers of cuckoos and crows,
and having offered a thousand oblations, one should then collect the ashes.
Having gathered them without distinction, one should form a fist containing the ashes.
Consecrated by this very [mantra] recited one hundred times:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate mahākālarudrāya tripuravināśanakāraṇāya daha daha dhama dhama paca paca matha matha mohaya mohaya unmādaya unmādaya ucchedaya ucchedaya śrīmahārudra*.
The Commanding One, the Sound-Maker, the Enchantress, the Blessed Lady—*kheṃ kheṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
By the scattering of ashes in either a village or a city, the destruction of enemies occurs; there is no doubt in this matter. (UT 2.26)
The ash has been cast away, yet it dwells within the city once more.
I shall explain the process of re-embodiment; listen to this yoga in brief, by the mere application of which one will become embodied again. (UT 2.27)
Having fashioned an image of the enemy bull using cow-dung mixed with the dust from his feet,
the wise one should consecrate it twenty-one times with this mantra. (2.28–2.29)
One should cut it with a sharp blade; then it will become a *kulva*.
Then the knower of mantras, for the purpose of dispatching those who have set out, should use this mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya kāmaprabhañjanāya amukaṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ svāhā*. (UT 2.30)
Having prepared honey mixed with clarified butter, one should apply it to this spot;
then, having bathed with cow's milk, one will become healthy. Now follows the procedure for causing madness.
The root of the golden seed (*kanakabīja*), powdered ghee,
the excrement of a house sparrow, and likewise the seed of the *karañja* tree—
this powder causes madness; by consuming it, one becomes insane.
And having consecrated it twenty-one times with this mantra, it should be given for consumption and drink; he will undoubtedly become insane.
Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya, [make so-and-so] insane, insane! Cchaḥ cchaḥ svāhā!
One should drink *śatapuṣpikā* with goat’s milk and blood,
or having drunk it with ghee, one then attains well-being. Thus ends the procedure for causing madness.
Salt that has been consecrated twenty-one times with mantras should be cooked over a fire of *karavīraka* wood by means of smoke.
Having taken that salt, the wise practitioner should reduce it to powder.
Food and drink consecrated with this mantra should be given;
having been consecrated one hundred times, it causes anyone—whether an enemy or whoever else—to become blind from eating it. There is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Oṃ, obeisance to Uḍḍāmareśvara; render the body blind, ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā!
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for causing leprosy, by the mere drinking of which a human being becomes leprous.

The juice of *bhallātaka*, *guñjā*, and *maṇḍalakārikā*, combined with a house-lizard, should be administered in food and drink. Within seven days, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) arises; once drunk, it increases further.
One should administer its pacification as spoken by Rudra:

the physician should give *dhātrī*, *khadira*, and *nimba* together with sugar, having ground them into a powder and combined them with honey and clarified butter for those who have digested their previous meal.
Rice cooked with milk (śālibhakta), patola, and milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee;
or warm mung-bean flour, or even rice combined with that—
by the mere giving of these, a person attains happiness.
Having collected an aquatic creature, a man should dry it in the sun;
then the wise one should cause it to be burned for the sake of that person whose life he desires.
With its limbs burning intensely, he should blow upon that creature which has lost consciousness.
If one desires his life, one should certainly wash the limb.
One should wash the powder from the base of the foot with sour gruel (kāñjika),
rub the penis with oil, and wash it with cold water.
By performing this, a person attains happiness.
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for subjugation and so forth, by the mere knowledge of which the world becomes one's servant. (UT 2.47)
The heart of a reciter of the Purāṇas is likewise permeated by leprosy.
If one should scatter powdered remains of offerings made to Śiva upon another's head,
that person will certainly remain his servant for as long as he lives.
Having recited this mantra seven times, the knower of mantras, using the following mantra—
*Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya svādhikāraṃ sādhaya sādhaya svāhā*—
[should prepare an ointment] with sandalwood, *tagara*, costus, *priyaṅgu*, and *nāgakesara*. (UT 2.50)
One should prepare equal parts of the five components of black dhattūra;
these should be made into pills in the shade and administered with food and drink.
This will bring a man or a woman under one's control for as long as they live.

Having consecrated it for seven days with this mantra, the knower of mantras [should use] *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *adhaḥpuṣpī*, and likewise *saṃkocapuṣpikā*. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the one garlanded with delusion! *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ* svāhā!
Śvetā and girikarṇī, both processed for seven days and combined with one's own semen,
should be administered in food and drink;
this is declared to be a subjugation [of the person] for as long as life lasts, without a doubt.
Vajra, or abhayā, lodhra, mañjiṣṭhā, hiṅgupattrikā,
divine vacā, viśālākṣā, and the very beautiful kambugrīvā—
by applying these as an ointment to the limbs with the bark of kumārī, [the body] shall measure seven cubits.
And on the tenth day, a certain mantra is recited;
there is no need for deliberation here regarding its power to cause one to fall asleep as if from poison.
In the midst of the water, my *vartikā* makes [the enemy] a thief. (UT 2.56–2.57)
One should administer curd, honey, fresh butter, long pepper, ginger, black pepper, and seventhly, rock salt;
indeed, if one has been bitten even by a wrathful Takṣaka, by drinking this remedy here, that poison shall become non-toxic at that very moment.
A plaster made of Kuṣṭha, Amṛtā, Ativiṣā, and Haridrā [is also effective].
This medicine spoken by Garuḍa removes poison and sustains life. [It consists of] the skins of an owl,
a jackal, a vulture, a buffalo, a cat,
a boar, a crow, and a frog.
One should have the eyes of a mouse ground into a fine powder;
indeed, one whose eyes are anointed with this may see at night as if by day.
This is the ritual mantra for these [substances]; without the mantra, it is not successful.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to Rudra, to Śiva, the Lord of lights; grant us lights for the sake of producing mental power, svāhā! Having stayed for one night, concentrated on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and having performed the worship of the *liṅga*, he should consecrate the water with mantras.

Standing in the southern direction, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Thereupon, the mantras and collyriums will be accomplished in every respect. "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Uḍḍāmareśvara! Grant me the accomplishment of the collyrium-mantra, svāhā! This concludes the section on the collyrium.
Now, regarding the method for becoming a *piśācī*:
having fumigated oneself with the seeds of *kanaka*, *priyaṅgu*, and likewise *guggulu*, one should enter the royal assembly.
One who inhales this yoga becomes completely submissive.
Likewise, the seeds of gold, white arka, candrakasara,
kuṣṭha, and devadāru— all these combined together— [are used].
Having ground [this] and smeared one's limbs with it, by means of the most powerful power of yoga,
wherever one enters, there one shall be victorious. (Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra 2.67)
The Third Chapter:
Having taken the two wings of a crow and a snake’s slough, combined with cremation-ground ashes, there shall be the eradication of the enemy. UT 3.1
Thus ends the section on eradication.
I shall now proclaim the discourse on spirits as spoken by Garuḍa, by the mere knowledge of which enemies come under one's control. (UT 3.2)
Having collected the resin of the *śatru* tree, its powder, and its essence,
one should infuse it for seven nights and administer it together with food.
By the mere giving of that, he will indeed be seized by *piśācas*.
For the purpose of restoring health, one should administer *jayā* and *madhuyaṣṭikā*.
One should soak the seeds of the *kataka* tree with the resins produced from the *śāla* tree for seven nights, and they are then administered together with food.
By merely consuming it, a person is seized by the *grahas*;
by drinking sugar and milk, one becomes healthy, and not otherwise.
[One should also take] the resin of *vāstuka* and the seeds of *kataka*.
Having been crushed and rendered stale, it is seized by the *brahmarākṣasas*.
By drinking milk mixed with sugar, one becomes healthy; otherwise, it is not so.
[One should also take] the seeds of the *mātuluṅga* with the exudation of *kapikacchu*.
One should perform the visualization for seven nights and cause [the medicine] to be administered with food and drink.
*Oṃ namo bhagavate uḍḍāmareśvarāya maheśvaro nāma svāhā*.
And [this should be done] with the powder of *āmalaka* together with women’s milk. (UT 3.9)
Having caused [the patient] to drink this, health will certainly arise.
One should give that powder— made from sugar, lotus filaments, and the pulp of lotus stamens—
all ground into a fine powder, together with milk.
Then the man becomes free from malevolent planets and restored to health.
(Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra, Chapter Four)
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare that which is very difficult to obtain in the discourse on spirits (bhūtavāda),
by the mere knowledge of which all success is produced:
Oṃ hrīṃ kālī kaṅkālī kila kila svāhā.
One should first recite this mantra ten thousand times;
thereafter, one should perform a thousand oblations, and Kaṅkālī will become a granter of boons, giving four māṣas of gold every day.
Now, for the paralyzing of the mouths of all people: *antaḥ oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavatī durvacatī kili vācābhañjanī sarvajanamukhastambhinī hrāṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*.
With this mantra, one should perform a thousand-fold oblation (*havana*) of *bilva* and black pepper smeared with ghee; all the people of the realm will become one's servants.
If, with this same mantra, one performs a thousand-fold oblation of *nyagrodha* fuel-sticks smeared with ghee, then women will be brought under control.
Oṃ rauṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ eṃ vada vada vāgvādinī vāgīśvarī namaḥ svāhā.
By reciting this mantra one thousand times, it produces poetic skill; there is no doubt about this.
*Oṃ oṃ oṃ īṃ īṃ īṃ aiṃ aiṃ aiṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
By reciting this mantra ten thousand times, it produces poetic skill. (UT 4.2)
Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra,
Fifth Chapter:
Listen, my son, I shall explain how [this] deludes the three worlds.
I shall tell you exactly how other men fall under one's control:
cardamom, costus, lodh, sweet flag, and red sandalwood,
combined with cremation-ground ashes— this is a practice that ends in death.
Killing is the act of contraction.
One should place equal parts of horse gram (*kulattha*), bilva leaf, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) in a copper vessel.
When the vessel has stood for seven nights, the wise man should cook oil with these [ingredients].
Having smeared the vulva with that oil, she approaches her husband;
having attained sexual union, the husband becomes a slave, and not otherwise.
The wise one should prepare pills with *nāgara* mixed with honey;
when combined with horse urine, it brings men under one's control.
Then, [one should take] saffron, *śatapuṣpā*, *priyaṅgu*, and *rocanā*.
If a wife should be unfortunate, she should be given [medicine] with goat’s milk;
thereby she will always become fortunate and attain service to her husband.
[One should take] the seeds of the citron and the fruits of the lotus.
One should apply red powder produced from the ocean together with honey;
by merely adding oil, the husband will certainly become a slave.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme essence of the yogas.
By merely knowing this, a woman becomes a servant.
Uśīra and sandalwood mixed with honey—
this is the "elephant-trunk" application, which brings all women under one's control.
One should apply saffron mixed with *śaśin* (camphor) to the vulva;
by this, her own [virginity] arises along with all its limbs, and the accumulation of the birth-canal is restored.
Clove, rock salt, honey, long pepper, and black pepper [are also used].
One should smear a man’s body with this; he will become like an elephant’s trunk.
One should grind together beeswax and *varaṭā* (a type of wasp) with cold water.
By merely being smeared with that, no orifice arises in the female organ.
In that case, by washing it, there will be the state of being able to conceive.
Having taken his own semen with his left hand at the end of sexual union,
he who smears it on the left foot of a woman shall bring her under his control.
She who touches the genitals of her beloved with her left foot while he is occupied with his enjoyments shall become his slave for as long as she lives; there is no doubt in this matter.
(UT 5.16) [A mixture of] pigeon droppings, rock salt, and licorice, taken in equal parts...
Whichever excellent woman one approaches after having smeared the *liṅga* with this, she shall become submissive.
Having ground together camphor, *tālīśapatra*, and the penis with honey,
and having smeared [the penis] with it, whichever woman one approaches will become submissive.
If one anoints the liṅga with these— rocanā, gold, the seed of Śambhu, camphor, and sandalwood— whomever one worships shall become submissive.
(Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra 5.19)

The sixth chapter: Having taken equal portions of the hair of a black goat, the hair of a black cat, and the feathers of a black crow, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or on a Saturday or Tuesday, under the asterism of Aśleṣā or Ārdrā, one should grind them with water from a well, a pond, or a river.
Having made a pill, one should sit in battle;
one should apply a tilaka-mark with the dust of the battlefield.
Immediately thereafter, whatever other men behold it will tremble, faint, leap up, and flee.
For those who grind [this] and apply it as an ointment, some pure substance falls upon them and does not leave;
this yoga, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been proclaimed by me—
I declare that it must never be revealed to anyone.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme knowledge of the body,
by the mere understanding of which the auspicious and inauspicious arise—
namely, life and death, gain and loss, victory and defeat.
Pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, as well as going and coming— these,
indeed, the daughter of Himālaya questioned the bull-bannered Lord.

Furthermore, regarding the principles (tattvas) of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, and the scriptures [taught] therein, by which yoga this triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, was brought into being through the great grace of the Guru.

Those whose combinations of gross and subtle [elements] are described, and that [combination] is observed in one's subsequent activity—what is the name of that, and what is the inquiry regarding it? As it is said according to the rule: "Then the five principles (pañcatattva) are recited.

Now, when a messenger arrives and speaks, his speech arises; having understood the syllables of the five principles, whichever principle-syllable appears in the mouth during the contemplation of the question [is the result].
He recites the *tattva*.

If, in the contemplation of the question, there are syllables of the earth-*tattva*, then it is the earth-*tattva*. If these are more numerous, then they are the water-*tattvas*; the meaning is that these are the syllables of the *tattvas*.
A Ā Ī ĪŪ Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ ḹ—these are the syllables of the earth element (pṛthvītattva).
E AI O AU AṂ AḤ—these are the syllables of the water element (jalatattva). Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña—these are the syllables of the fire element (tejastattva).

Ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma—these are the syllables of the air element (vāyutattva). Ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha—these are the syllables of the space element (ākāśatattva).
These become additional syllables through the process of expansion.
One must understand the various kinds of thoughts and the even and uneven syllables as the *pṛthvī-tattva* (earth element).
Furthermore, life and death, gain and loss, victory and defeat, pleasure and pain, coming and going—whatever is even or uneven, these are to be discerned as the *aptattva* (water element).
When the mind is directed toward the subject matter of a performed speech or toward the earth element, then the syllables of the water element arise; at that time, one recites what has been chanted.
When the syllables of the earth-element (pṛthivītattva) arise within non-conceptualization (apracintā), then the earth-element exists;
the same should be understood for the others as well.
These are the syllables by which one speaks.

When the syllables of fire (tejas) and space (ākāśa) predominate in the consideration of gain, then that inauspiciousness will become even greater. When there is movement from one's country or from reality, or when setting out on a journey—such as traveling to a village or going to battle—if the syllables of fire predominate in the *ahetu*, *ake*, and *ḍake* [divisions], they are predominant.
Regarding earth, water, fire, air, and space, these are their respective syllables; at the time of marriage, among these, the syllables of fire bring about auspiciousness.
Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra,
Seventh Chapter:
Now, the preparation of medicinal herbs is described.
This herb is supreme and most excellent; it must be guarded with great effort.
By the mere application of it, even deities come under one's control.
This herb is declared by the wise to be the world-renowned *cāṇḍālī*.
Worshipped by the hosts of gods and asuras, she accomplishes all purposes and goals.
O Goddess, by this procedure, she moves upon four feet, being one-leaved, two-leaved, three-leaved, and four-leaved.

When employed specifically for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarman*), it brings women under control when combined with the impurities from one's own body as a single leaf; with two leaves, it brings kings and royal officials under control;

with three leaves together with *śrīśāka* and black pepper, it brings a wicked army under control; and with four leaves together with a bulbous root (*kanduka*), it brings a rutting and wicked elephant under control.

Now the procedure for uprooting is described: having become pure on a Saturday, having performed the evening twilight rites and so forth, and having performed worship and other rites with the five offerings of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food-offerings, one should take unbroken rice and fruit in hand, stand near the medicinal plant, and perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*). Then, before the sun has risen, one should dig it up using a small wedge of *khadira* wood.
In this regard, the mantra is: "By that [power] with which Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, Maheśvara, Śacīpati, Pitṛpati, Jaleśa, and Dhanādhipa dig you up—with that I shall cause you to be dug up;
stay, stay, O great medicinal herb!"
Having recited thus, one should dig [the site].

Beginning at dawn while pure and in a secluded place, the medicinal herbs should be gathered according to the release of the mantra for the sake of accomplishment; for they do not become like mere wood.
Homage be to you, O you who are born of the deathless, who increase strength and vigor!
Grant me strength and long life; carry my evil far away.
By this mantra, having dug [the earth] and performed the uprooting, whoever was previously brought here should become otherwise.
Stay right here, O auspicious one; become the cause of my emaciation. Once my task is accomplished and perfected, you shall indeed depart from here.
*Oṃ hīṃ raktacāmuṇḍe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Under this mantra, during the Puṣya or Hasta constellation, all medicinal herbs should be uprooted. For those men by whom these herbs are dug, uprooted, or produced when the sun has risen, their potency and power become diminished through the influence of being drunk in by the rays of the sun; they do not bring about success.
If they are uprooted when the sun has risen, then their worship must be performed.
Having smeared an area of one and a quarter cubits with red hibiscus, red lotuses, red oleanders, red sandalwood, saffron, and cow dung from a cow, one should fashion a square in its center.
Within that, one should worship the Sun, a circle measuring one span in diameter, using red sandalwood and saffron.
One should worship the planets, beginning with the Moon, at the sides.
Then, one should offer a *bali* oblation with red rice, flowers, and red [pigments], using the mantra to be recited hereafter:
*Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ draiṃ drauṃ draḥ saḥ svāhā*.
Having performed worship with this mantra, one should uproot [the target]; she becomes endowed with vigor and capable of accomplishing all tasks.
*Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra*, Chapter Eight.
Now I shall further explain the method for women to conceive.
Any woman who drinks lotus seeds with cow’s milk will truly become pregnant. On a Sunday one should invite [the practitioner], and on a Monday one should consume [the medicine].
At the time of her menses, she should eat the root of the *śarīṣa* plant situated in the eastern direction together with cow’s ghee; after one year, she will become pregnant.

And whatever woman is childless, if she should always eat a wood-apple (*kapittha*) after it has been consecrated with this mantra, she too shall become possessed of a son. A woman who has bathed on the bank of a solitary tree should likewise consecrate [the fruit] with the mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, even one who is barren from the very beginning shall indeed become pregnant.
Wherever Lord Śiva may be, even in the absence of a confluence of rivers,
in that river and in that direction, O Svāhā, the barren woman shall become possessed of sons.
The procedure is stated here: having first carefully smeared the ground with the dung of a tawny cow, and having bathed according to the prescribed method, one should then construct a mandala.
It should be square with four corners, and a circle is prescribed in its center.
Afterwards, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the center of that.
One should worship the Deity in the middle and worship the Śakti on the petals.
A wise person should place a flawless lotus in front of the maṇḍala.
One should draw [the image] with the color of a peacock-feather claw. [The clay should consist of:

earth from the seven mountain ranges of the Bhṛṅgītāku family, one's own excrement and urine, earth from an anthill, earth from the root of a nimba tree, gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, the roots of a thousand [plants], all sacred fords, all oceans, all rivers, and all medicinal herbs.

One should, with a steady mind, arrange all the deities, all the siddhis, all the yoginīs, all the mountains, all the nāgas, the five kinds of fruits, the five types of unbroken grains (akṣata), and the five golden flowers within the consecrated flask.
Now, the mantra is: *kṣaṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*.

By this mantra and according to this rite, a woman who has abandoned her vows, one who is unchaste, a goddess, a barren woman, one who has been abandoned by five husbands, or one who is childless, shall obtain sons; and an unfortunate woman shall become fortunate.
By this very rite, a maiden obtains a virtuous husband.
Those who employ mantras and medicinal herbs, and others who use powders and incense, as well as those who perform cruel acts of sorcery— when their bodies are purified, they become pure.
And whatever other Rākṣasas roam the earth as creators of obstacles [are likewise purified].
All these go to dissolution; this, O Goddess, is the truth spoken by me.
When the mantra is uttered even once, great merit is produced;
sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to destruction—of this there is no doubt.
Now the first method is described: one should drink ten *māṣakas* of *nāgakeśara* together with cow’s ghee on the day of her ritual bath after menstruation.
Immediately thereafter, she should engage in union with her husband at night;
she will certainly become pregnant.
Now, the second method: one *māṣa* of white cumin (*śvetajīraka*) should be placed with water in an earthen vessel in an open place throughout the night.

On a day when there is fire [in the hearth], it should be ground on a stone; then, on the day of her ritual bath following menstruation (*ṛtusnāna*), whichever woman drinks this with water that has stood overnight and engages in union with her husband at night, she will certainly become pregnant.

Now, the third method: *dakālvadmadīpikā*. If one drinks ten *māṣakas* [of the powder] together with cow's milk on the day of the ritual bath following menstruation (*ṛtusnāna*) and engages in union with her husband that night, she will certainly become pregnant.
This is the third method.
"Oṃ ghaṇṭākarṇāya svāhā. Having recited this seven times, one may enter a village or a city; there, one obtains excellent food.
Furthermore, O Alla, it is accomplished by this: one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
Then, having sprinkled clay from the root of a *śirīṣa* tree at the four corners of the field, the mouths of rabbits, mice, boars, quadrupeds, and so forth, will be bound.
Now I shall fully declare the mantras that grant me fruit— those which, when practiced for no less than ten [days], bring about accomplishment and bestow liberation.
[I shall also explain] the characteristics of the enemy, the friend, the neutral, the one to be accomplished, and the one already accomplished.

Having written the syllables of the mantra, when the first consonant class (varga) letter of that practitioner occurs, it is a friend; when the second class letter occurs, it is accomplished (siddha);

when it belongs to the third class, it is to be accomplished (sādhya); when the fourth class letter occurs, it is neutral (udāsīna); and when the fifth class letter occurs, it should be known as an enemy.

Having understood these distinctions, one should then begin the purification of the mantra; this brings happiness to practitioners. Now, the roots of the grove of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), which have been washed, should be consecrated in black mustard seeds mixed with cow's curd.
Thereafter, one should consume them according to the prescribed rules.
"One should apply this [formula] to one's own mouth during times free from disease;
'I shall declare its ritual procedure,' said the Goddess.
Now, the mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ ṣaṇmukhāya śaktihastāya mayūravāhanāya auṣadhīkena dehi me bhava svāhā*."
Having become pure on the fourteenth day, one should extract a peacock’s crest with this mantra; then it becomes endowed with great power.
If it is collected together with cow’s ghee, then one becomes possessed of the strength of the senses. With the five impurities, one becomes a goldsmith.

Furthermore, the root of white karavīra, the root of white girikarṇikā, and the root of hevacanā, combined with the five impurities (pañcamala) and formed into a hollowed palm (añjali), should be administered in food and drink; this brings about subjugation until death.
Furthermore, one should take the root of the white mountain karṇikā together with its own potency, and the root of the white arka together with the potency of its own five-fold impurity;

having combined these under the asterism of Hasta or Puṣya, one should grind them with the hands of a virgin and, on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, form a pill with elephant ichor to be held in the hand.
To whomsoever even a single [offering] is given, she becomes submissive; it is not otherwise.

Even to snakes an offering is given during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and those snakes also become submissive, according to the word of the illustrious Mahābhairava. When an offering is made together with saffron (kuṅkuma), then indeed the elephant becomes submissive.
When a tilaka is made with gorocanā and saffron together, then that woman wanders following behind one.
A sectarian mark (*tilaka*) should not be shown to the wives of one's guru.
At the king’s gate, in legal proceedings, at a wedding, and in a battle that brings victory, this [mark] is the "Deluder of the Three Worlds.

Take five *māṣas* of *triphalā*, one *māṣa* of *nimba*, two *māṣas* of *kadamba*, three *māṣas* of *nīpa*, four *māṣas* of *tirāitā*, five *māṣas* of *karañja*, six *māṣas* of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and seven *māṣas* of *mayūraśikhā*; these should be taken in equal proportions.
One should have it made into fine powders;
immediately thereafter, one should grind them with honey.
One may then take food according to one's appetite; of this there is no doubt.
This powder is difficult to obtain even for the gods.

If this night-powder and the powder of *śirīṣa* bark are given with cow’s ghee to a woman on the day of her ritual bath following menstruation for her to drink, that woman—even if barren—will become pregnant;
there is no doubt about this.
If a woman who is childless consumes this powder together with the fruit of the *kapittha* tree during her fertile period, she obtains a son.

This powder—consisting of equal parts of the root of white *kaṅkolī* and the powder of *lakṣmaṇā*—should be given for constant consumption during the fertile period along with a decoction of saffron; by that, purification of her body occurs.
Afterwards, she should consume it for five days during the period of her menses; then she becomes capable of conceiving—of this there is no doubt.
(Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra, Ninth Chapter)
Now I shall proclaim another medicine, most difficult to obtain,
known by the name Āsphoṭī and renowned as Nāgadamanī.
I will describe its ritual procedure, which is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to attain.
All poisons perish by anointing [with it] or by consuming it in an instant.

Having smeared that [root] on the palm of the hand, a snake can be held; as soon as it is held, the snake does not perish. By anointing the wounds with the mantra honored by the Nāgas, the snake is destroyed. By digging up the root of the *nāgadamanī* and applying it to the veins or the forehead, it destroys [the poison] on all sides. Rheumatism caused by phlegm (*āmavāta*), rheumatism caused by bile (*pittavāta*), and rheumatism caused by wind (*śleṣmavāta*)—these winds are destroyed by consuming it; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now I shall describe the methods and the reasons for the preparation of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhī*).

A son is a means of subjugation; even a timid woman, by giving even a single seed of this "son of sons" (*putraputra*)—namely, *kaṃsa*—to a man, brings him completely under her control. She abandons her husband and wanders about naked while the people look on.
Now I shall describe the tantric procedure.

That which is called by the people "the copper pedestal" (*tāmravedīparora*) should be consecrated on a Saturday; having become naked and with disheveled hair, one should take it up before the sun has risen.

Having ground it properly with the five impurities (*pañcamala*) of a woman and, being overcome by passion, having mixed it with betel leaf and given it to one's sister, she becomes submissive; it is not otherwise.
Even a mother, having abandoned her son and become intent upon him, follows after him naked wherever he may be; of this there is no doubt.

There is a great medicinal herb known as *kākajaṅghā* which exists everywhere in every village. On a Saturday at the time of twilight, one should perform its consecration (*abhimantraṇa*). Then, rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta* before the sun has risen under the *puṣya* asterism, [one should proceed].
Or, under the asterism of Hasta, one should uproot that [plant] together with its roots using a stake of *khadira* wood.
Then, on the seventh, eighth, or ninth lunar day— these being joined with the asterisms of Punarvasu, Puṣya, or Hasta—
one should grind it together with one's own excrement, and having added one's own semen and one's own blood to it, for whichever woman...

That woman who is given [this] becomes submissive; this is indeed the truth. One should consecrate [the offering] with this mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavati tripure trailokyamohini aiṃ drāṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauṃ, quickly bring [the woman] named so-and-so under my control, svāhā*.
This is the mantra.

Now the ritual manual for *guñjā* is written: On a Saturday at the time of twilight, one should consecrate white *guñjā* with mantras. Then, rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, before the sun has risen, one should become naked and, using a stake of *khadira* wood, uproot the plant together with its roots under the asterism of Puṣya or Hasta, along with the menses of a woman and a mixture of *gorocana*, saffron from Kashmir, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, musk, camphor, and the ichor of an elephant.
Having consecrated it with this mantra, one should apply the *tilaka*; then a woman, deluded by the arrows of desire, becomes overwhelmed.
One should consecrate it with this mantra: *oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the *Kāmabāṇatilaka*.
Now, having extracted the essence, the subjugation and delusion rites mentioned in other tantras are briefly written;
some of that which generates delight for those possessed by desire is also spoken here.
(UT 9.3) Among these, first is the procedure for the *tilaka*.
If a man grinds together *lajjā*, *madhūka*, *kavya*, and the root of the *nalini* lotus with his own semen and applies it as a *tilaka*,
he brings the three worlds under his control at that very moment.
The sage Vātsyāyana has proclaimed this unsurpassed yoga:
white [mustā], aṣṭamūla, mañjiṣṭhā, vacā, mustā, and kuṣṭha—
having combined these with the blood from a woman’s womb, one should apply them to the forehead.
He who applies this auspicious mark (*tilaka*) will, in due course, bring the three worlds under his control;
being grateful, he shall make them subject to his will and rejoice for a long time upon the earth.
[The ingredients are: *tagara*, the root of *pippalī*, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *kaṇā*, and *jaṭā*.
Having brought these together with his own five limbs into a single unity,
the wise man who applies a tilaka with honey on the day of Mars shall bring the entire world under his control; of this there is no doubt.
She who prepares *gorocanā* with the blood of her own man and applies it as a mark (*tilaka*) on her forehead will greatly delude her husband. Now follows the procedure for collyrium (*añjana*).

On the day of the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī), one who applies collyrium fallen from the head of a man in a cremation ground as eye-salve shall delude the entire world. Purifying yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kesara), a virgin (kanyā), and realgar (śilā)— UT_9.11 [The practitioner] purifies these [substances].
One should cause [the victim] to sacrifice; everything that comes within the range of his vision will be utterly deluded.
Having prepared a wick from *tālīśa*, *kuṣṭha*, and *nāgara*, one should place it in mustard oil and [apply] soot upon the head of a man.

If one applies collyrium [made from] *śilā*, *kiñjalka*, *phalinī*, and *rocanā* to his eyes, he will always become like a servant to everyone who comes within the range of his vision throughout the three worlds. (UT 9.14)
"Prepared during the conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, this is the supreme means of enchanting a couple.
Thus [ends the section]. Now follows the procedure for the powder (*cūrṇavidhi*):
*kākajaṅghā*, realgar (*śilā*), the two wings of a bee, and black lotus.

The powder of *tagara* and these [other substances], when thrown, causes delusion. The powder of the excrement of a man suffering from wind-bile (*vātapaittika*) and of a *mālāsava* [insect] belonging to the *pakṣāvali* [class], when thrown upon the head, causes delusion.
Now follows the procedure for consumption:
having extracted all the entrails and so forth from the belly of a wagtail (*khañjarīṭa*) and filling it with one's own semen, one should place it around the neck of a dog. (UT 9.18)
Having formed the mudrā, the wise one should retain it in solitude for seven days;
afterwards, having extracted and purified it, he should make a pill and dry it thoroughly.
By the method of consuming that, there is a mutual row of lamps.

This supreme observance is proclaimed as that which generates love between husband and wife. Another [method] is well-considered; now I shall further explain another *tilaka* that fulfills all desires.

Having taken equal parts of *gorocanā*, bamboo manna (*vaṃśalocana*), fish gall (*matsyapitta*), Kashmiri saffron, the filaments of saffron, the flower of the self-arisen deity (*svayambhūkusuma*), one’s own semen, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, musk, camphor, and the root of the *kākajaṅghā* plant, one should grind them with water from a well, a pond, or a river; having formed a pill the size of a girl’s earlobe,
one should dry the pill in the shade.
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with that [substance], whichever woman one looks upon becomes submissive.

With this mantra—*drauṃ vāṃ dhāṃ kṣauṃ aṃ kaṃ chaḥ*—one should consecrate a stake made of buffalo bone, nineteen finger-breadths long, by reciting it a thousand times; if one buries it at the edge of a well while uttering the name of someone, that person will be killed by a buffalo.

*Oṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ ḷṃ amukaṃ huṃ īṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ oṃ.* With this mantra, one should empower a three-finger-long stake made of peacock bone a thousand times and bury it at a crossroads in the name of whomever [one intends]. That person will wander there; they remain and roam about right there. By simply pulling it out, peace is restored in an instant.
Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ vrāṃ vrīṃ īṃ īṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ svāhā.

With this mantra, one should consecrate a twelve-finger-long stake made of ram bone a thousand times; wherever one buries it in someone's house, all their accomplishments (*siddhi*) become unattainable.
In the Lamp of Mantras, one should meditate on [the deity] resembling the Bandhūka flower, with the syllable *drīṃ*.
O lady of excellent hips, listen; I shall tell you of the sixfold [result] through *kumbhaka*.
By meditating for one month, one will certainly bring a great woman;
in one month, by means of this mantra, one may bring a daughter of the *nāgas*.
A celestial maiden [is attained] in three months at evening; it cannot be otherwise.
With this very mantra, *oṃ haṃ haḥ*, the wrathful sacrificers (*krodhayājaka*) are to be meditated upon. (UT 9.23)
O Goddess of the gods, for one who performs the sacrifice, [the world] resembling Rudra with the hand of Rudra [is reached] by the gods and asuras;
the human world in one month, the world of the Nagas in two months,
and the heavenly world in three months— of this there is no doubt.
Through the practice of six months, make the three worlds motionless.
Oṃ raktahaṭā raktagaṭā mukuṭadhāriṇī edhati svāhā!
This is the king of mantras, the reversed piercer.

*Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ dhṛīṃ vikṛtānanā bāhye phaṭ svāhā.* Having written this mantra upon a yantra, if it is shown to anyone, he will be seized by an irregular fever occurring every day, every two days, or every three days; it is destroyed at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. *Oṃ bandhuna kṣayaṃ drīṃ drīṃ amukasyātmānaṃ nityajvareṇa pattrībandhanamātrasya sphura svāhā.*
Thus ends the leaf for purifying chronic fever.
*Oṃ kṣaḥ svāhā*.
Having thoroughly consecrated water with this mantra, one should sprinkle the body of the feverish person; by that, liberation from fever will certainly occur.
The instruction for one whose mount is a donkey-lion follows in due order:
Vāyu, mounted upon a bear-steed, roars like a thundercloud.
On a Sunday, having written this verse, one should place it upon one's head.

By merely establishing it, one removes a fever lasting three months. Then, having taken the blood of a wild cat and a wick made from lotus fiber, one should saturate them seven times [with the juice].
Then, one should cause soot to fall before Śiva using the oil produced from that;
with eyes anointed by that, one certainly becomes invisible. *Uttaratantra* 9.29: *hebhirihebherihe*.
Having taken water with this [mantra], having looked at it, and having recited it one thousand times, success is achieved in three nights by means of this very collyrium.
One should cause soot to fall from a wick made of lotus fibers using oil; one whose eyes are anointed with that becomes invisible.
Then, having washed the eyes with cow urine, one becomes visible once again. (UT 9.30)
Now, the mantra for subduing the ḍākinīs: Akṣaḥ, kṣāṃ, kṣaukājasinau; the deity is Tattvadhūlinī; Ghonāśālinī;
Bhamantri; Bandhuśanādaivataṃ; with the small thorn (laghukaṇṭaka), the one who commands the city; the deity Mahābhairava; the maṇḍala; Acala; oṃ cchaḥ cchaḥ cchaḥ; ḍākinīmatabandhu; namaḥ.
Oṃ namo bhagavate vajrāya caṇḍeśvarāya īṃ īṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the mantra for subduing all *bhūtas* and *ḍākinīs*.
"Damana, *sarpa-laṅga*, *ebha-lisiṃ*, *aja-bandhani-śi*, *nāgapāśa*, *acalaḥ*": this is the mantra for subduing and binding.
Oṃ raṃ strīṃ, quickly ha svāhā!
Having written [the name] of Tripurā upon a leaf of the *udanāla* plant with vermilion and powdered conch-shell, one should purify it; within three days, she will come and meet with the fever.
Oṃ ahohaḥ, quickly bring [the woman] named so-and-so, svāhā! This is the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). UT 9.31.
Oṃ strīṃ strīṃ valīṃ valīm īṃ ahaḥ phaṭ svāhā! One becomes healthy after bathing.
O Apsaraṇī, let [the woman] named so-and-so live!
Having consecrated water seven times with this mantra, it should be given to the woman one desires for her to drink. *Oṃ namo jale mohe kule phalāni saṃkule svāhā*.
He to whom that which is empowered seven times with this mantra is given becomes submissive.

Oṃ namo jale mohe drāṃ abjini phaṭ svāhā. By means of this mantra, one should wash one’s face with water at dawn; one will become beloved by all people and a master of all accomplishments. Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā.
Having consecrated betel-leaf with this mantra, whoever it is given to becomes submissive:

*Oṃ namo jale mohe hana hana daha daha paca paca matha matha amukaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā*. Now follows the practice for the Yakṣiṇī-mantra: Surasundarī, Manohāriṇī, Kanakāvatī, Ratikarī, Kāmeśvarī, Naṭyanurāgiṇī, and Padminī—these eight Yakṣiṇīs are the means for accomplishing one's desires.
Now follows the sādhana of Surasundarī: *Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha surasundari svāhā*.

Having gone to the abode of Vajrapāṇi and offered guggulu incense, one should worship her at the three junctions of the day. One should recite the mantra a thousand times at each of the three junctions for the duration of a month; then, within that month, she becomes manifest. On the final day, one should offer an arghya oblation with red sandalwood.
Then, having arrived, she becomes a mother, a sister, or a wife; she performs exactly those actions appropriate to each.
If she is a mother, she then gives perfected substances and elixirs (*rasāyana*).
If she is a sister, she then gives priceless clothing, as before.
If she becomes one's wife, she then fulfills all prosperity;
however, one must avoid sleeping with another woman here, for she is fond of sexual union, and otherwise she perishes.
Now follows the sādhana of Manohāriṇī: oṃ hīṃ āgaccha āgaccha manohari svāhā.

Having gone here to the confluence of rivers, one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste, offer agallochum incense, and recite the mantra one thousand times every day for the duration of a month.
Then, at the end of the month, one should present an *arghya* offering of sandalwood water; with a single-minded focus on flowers and fruit, one must perform worship to her.
Thereupon, at the time of midnight, she will certainly arrive; once arrived, she carries out his command and gives him a hundred pieces of gold.
She grants [boons] to the practitioner every day.
Now, for the practice of Kanakāvatī: *Oṃ hrīṃ kanakāvati maithunapriye āgaccha āgaccha svāhā*.

Standing near a banyan tree, one should offer an oblation of liquor, meat, and so forth to her with the root mantra, and having partaken of the remainder oneself, one should recite the root mantra one thousand times.
One should perform this for up to seven days.
On the night of the eighth day, at the time of midnight, she arrives accompanied by eight attendants, adorned with garments and ornaments.
Once arrived, she should be desired; she becomes a wife and provides clothing, ornaments, and food for twelve people. She constantly bestows eight *kalās* upon the practitioner.

Now follows the sādhana of Kāmeśvarī: *oṃ hīṃ āgaccha āgaccha kāmeśvari svāhā*. Having drawn an image in the form of a woman upon a birch-bark leaf with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and having worshipped it with either the sixteen or the five offerings (*upacāras*), one should then sit alone in a secluded place upon a bed, become single-minded, and recite [the mantra] a thousand times. Thereafter...
At the end of the month, with that same intention, one should worship one's own wife.
Then, having lit a lamp with honey and clarified butter every night, and subsequently observing silence, one should recite the root mantra one thousand times.
Thereafter, she will certainly arrive at the time of midnight; however, other women must be avoided.
Now, the sādhana for Ratipriyā: Oṃ hīṃ, come, come, O creator of delight, svāhā!

On this cloth, she should be painted in her variegated form, adorned with garments and golden ornaments, holding a blue lotus in her hand, and [depicted as] a young maiden. One should perform worship with jasmine flowers and offer incense of guggulu. Then, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times every day.

At the end of the month, one should perform worship according to the rules; incense and lamps should be lit. Then, at the time of midnight, she certainly arrives. Once arrived, she should be enjoyed in her female form; she becomes the practitioner’s wife, protects his retinue, and provides divine, desirable food.
And he gives [it].
Now, the practice for Padminī: *Oṃ hīṃ āgaccha āgaccha padmini svāhā*.

Having drawn a maṇḍala with sandalwood paste in one's own home, one should cause her to stand upon it; having offered incense of guggulu, one should recite the mantra one thousand times every day. Then, at the end of the month, on the night of the full moon—
Having performed the worship according to the rules, one should recite the mantra.

At the end of the recitation, at the time of midnight, she certainly arrives. Once arrived, she should be enjoyed; having become his wife, she grants all desires. She bestows upon the practitioner daily elixir, rejuvenation, and perfected substances.
Now, the *sādhana* of Naṭī: Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha naṭi svāhā.

Having gone there beneath an *aśoka* tree, and having offered food such as fish and meat, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and a *bali* offering, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. Then, at the end of a month, she will certainly come. Once arrived, she becomes a mother, a sister, or a wife.
If she becomes one's mother, then she gives divine, desire-granting food, and she also gives garments, perfumes, and a hundred pieces of gold.
If she becomes one's sister, then she brings and gives a most excellent woman from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
If she becomes one's wife, then within eight days she gives divine garments and an elixir.
Now, the sādhana for Anurāgiṇī: Oṃ hrīṃ anurāgiṇi āgaccha āgaccha svāhā.

Here, having drawn an image resembling a woman on birch bark with Kashmiri saffron, having performed the invocation and other rites, having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, and having presented betel leaves, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day.

One should recite [the mantra] three times a day for one month. At the end of the month, on the full moon day, having performed worship according to the rules and lit a lamp of ghee, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night.
Then, at the time of dawn, she will certainly arrive; once arrived, she grants all desires, bestows divine elixirs, and gives a thousand *dīnāras* every day.
Through her grace, one's lifespan shall extend for thousands of years.
Now, the thirty-six yakṣiṇīs:
Vicitrā, Vibhramā, Haṃsī, Bhīṣaṇī, Janarañjinī, Viśālā, Madanā, Ghaṇṭā, Kālakarṇī, and Mahābhayā. (UT 9.41)
Māhendrī, Śaṅkhinī, Cāndrī, Śmaśānā, Vaṭayakṣiṇī, Mekhalā, Vikalā, Lakṣmī, Mālinī, Śatapattrikā,
Sulocanā, Suśobhāḍhyā, Kapālinī, and Viśālinī.
Naṭī, Kāmeśvarī, Svarṇarekhā, and Surasundarī;
Manoharā, Pramodānurāgiṇī, Nakhakeśikā,
Bhāminī, Padminī, Svarṇāvatī, and Ratipriyā.
These thirty-six yakṣiṇīs, who bestow the desired accomplishments,
have been described at length by Mahādeva in the Karaṅkiṇīmata Tantra.
I shall now briefly explain their great method of propitiation.
And indeed, as they are satisfied, they bestow the fruit with composure.
One should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times, pure, at the foot of a banyan tree;
thereafter, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *campaka* flowers mixed with honey and clarified butter.
The practitioner of mantra should perform [the rite] one-tenth as prescribed by Śaṅkara;
then, O Goddess, she becomes perfected, wondrous, and the granter of desires. *Oṃ vicitre citrarūpiṇi me siddhiṃ kuru 2 svāhā*.
This is the mantra.
One should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times at night in a secluded cremation ground;
when the fire-oblation has been performed with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter in a tenth part of that number, [the rite is complete].
Vibhramā attains satisfaction when accompanied by fifty men;
she bestows food and wealth every day—so Śaṅkara has said.
Oṃ hrīṃ vibhrame, O you whose form is the essence of delusion, create delusion, create delusion! O Blessed One, svāhā!
Then, in a region of the city, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
when a fire-oblation has been performed with lotus petals mixed with ghee in a tenth part of that number,
the female swan bestows an ointment by which one perceives hidden treasures.
One grasps that [mantra] with ease and is not overcome by obstacles:
*oṃ drīṃ namo haṃsi haṃsavāhinī klīṃ klīṃ svāhā*.
Standing at the confluence of the three paths (*tripathastha*), one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times, followed by a tenth part of that for the concluding rites.
Oṃ śrīṃ drīṃ, O dweller in the banyan tree, born of the Yakṣa lineage, O Vaṭayakṣiṇī, come, come, svāhā!
If one recites this mantra beneath a Madhūka tree for a period of fourteen days,
Mekhalā, being pleased, bestows the supreme collyrium.
Oṃ drīṃ huṃ, obeisance and svāhā to Madanamekhalā, the mocker of passion.
A man should recite this mantra for three months while staying within a cave;
then, O Goddess, she becomes perfected, free from defects, and grants all desires. (UT 9.54)

Oṃ vikale aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ svāhā. Residing in his own home, the practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times with red karavīra flowers, followed by a tenth part of the total as an oblation of dūrvā grass and clarified butter.
When performed at home, the yakṣiṇī named Lakṣmī becomes accomplished; she bestows divine elixirs, alchemy, and hidden treasures. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ lakṣmi kamaladhāriṇi haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ svāhā.
Standing at a crossroads during a time of adversity, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times;
the Mālinī becomes perfected and bestows a divine sword,
by the power of which one may obtain a kingdom that is difficult to attain in this world.
Oṃ drīṃ oṃ, obeisance to Mālinī! Come, come, O beautiful one! O Haṃsahaṃsī, fulfill my desire; grant me union, svāhā!
If a sage recites this mantra one hundred thousand times in a grove of lotuses, having perfected it through oblations of milk and ghee, she grants him success and a treasure of the earth.
Oṃ drīṃ śatapattrike drīṃ drīṃ śrīṃ svāhā. Standing on the bank of a river, the practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times;
when a fire sacrifice with ghee is performed using one-tenth of that number, the Goddess becomes pleased.
She grants a sandal to him according to his desire in the sky;
with the speed of mind and wind, the practitioner goes and returns. Oṃ drīṃ klīṃ sulocane, grant me success, grant it, svāhā!
The practitioner, wearing red garments, should recite [the mantra] for a period of fourteen days;
then the goddess Śobhanā, the bestower of enjoyments, will become accomplished.
Oṃ drīṃ, O Śobhanā, with the aśoka sprout in the palm of your hand, śrīṃ kṣaḥ svāhā!
The practitioner who observes the great vow and subsists on meals of *śāli* rice should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times; then the sage obtains a skull-cup,
travels through the sky, and encounters [beings] from afar in the form of dreams.
"Vision from afar," and so forth—this he bestows upon the practitioner.
*Oṃ aiṃ kapālinī drāṃ drīṃ klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ klaiṃ klauṃ klaḥ haṃsaḥ so 'haṃ sakalahrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The teacher should recite this mantra fifty thousand times on the bank of a river.
When oblations are made with guggulu resin smeared with clarified butter, the Goddess becomes the bestower of good fortune.
*Oṃ varayakṣiṇī varayakṣaviśālini āgaccha 2 priyaṃ me bhavatu haime bhava svāhā.* Having gone beneath a holy Aśoka tree, one should prepare a beautiful mandala with sandalwood.
Having prepared [the offerings], one should worship the Goddess, offering a thousand incense sticks.
One should propitiate the mantra for a month, eating only at night and always subsisting on meat broth.
Having performed the auspicious worship at night, one who observes the vow of a sage should recite the mantra.
The actress goddess, having arrived, bestows upon the practitioner a treasure, mercury, and collyrium,
as well as a mantra and a divine yoga that grants success:
*Oṃ drīṃ naṭi mahānaṭi rūpavati drīṃ svāhā*.

Seated on a single seat in a pure place, one should recite the mantra three thousand times during each of the three junctions of the day for one month; then, one should commence the worship with flowers,
incense, food offerings, and lamps filled with ghee.

Having worshipped the Goddess at night, one with a clear mind should recite the mantra. When midnight has passed, the Goddess, having arrived, bestows divine elixir (*rasāyana*), garments, and ornaments.
Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha āgaccha kāmeśvari svāhā.
Having fashioned a beautiful and auspicious maṇḍala with sandalwood on the pleasant bank of a river,
one should worship the Goddess and then recite the mantra ten thousand times.
For twenty-one days, the goddess, being well-pleased, shall always bestow upon him a thousand dīnāras once midnight has passed;
she grants this to him every day, and he should spend it day by day.
Because there is no depletion of that [wealth], he does not give further and becomes angry.
*Oṃ hīṃ sarvakāmade manohare svāhā*.
Having arisen at midnight, one should recite this mantra a thousand times.
Then, after one month, the goddess will certainly reveal a treasure.
Oṃ hrīṃ pramodāyai svāhā!
Having drawn the well-characterized goddess upon birch bark with saffron, [one should worship her].

Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight, having honored the Goddess with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times at the three junctions of the day for one month; thereafter, having performed worship at night, one should recite it again.
When midnight has passed, the goddess arrives and,
being well-pleased, grants one thousand *dīnāras* every day.
*Oṃ anurāgiṇi maithunapriye yakṣakulaprasūte svāhā*.
Having gone to the abode of birds, the minister should worship with his nails and hair.
Having performed worship for twenty-one days, then at night,
the minister, well-restrained and single-minded, should repeat the mantra.
At midnight, the Goddess comes and grants the desired object:
*Oṃ hīṃ nakhakeśike svāhā*. For three days, one should abstain from food during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
With the mind focused upon it, one should recite [the mantra] from the moment of contact until liberation;
then that goddess, being pleased, bestows the supreme collyrium.
Anointed with that, a person sees treasures hidden beneath the earth that are otherwise invisible.
Oṃ hīṃ yakṣiṇi bhāmini ratipriye svāhā!
Having prepared an excellent maṇḍala with sandalwood at the foot of a *vaṭa* tree,
one should worship the yakṣiṇī and present an offering of food.
Then, one should recite the mantra over hare meat, ghee, and a cloth,
one thousand times each day for seven days.
Then, [the deity] will always come to him and grant the supreme ointment-mantra.
By whose power one may behold every treasure without hesitation:
*Oṃ hrīṃ āgaccha 2 svarṇāvati svāhā*.
Because on a cloth smeared with conch-shell powder, one sees the goddess Gaurī holding a blue lotus. (UT 9.85)
Having painted a divine image adorned with all ornaments, a person should worship it;
then, having honored it with *jātī* flowers, they should recite [the mantra] one thousand times. Thereafter, the knower of mantras should perform auspicious worship of her for seven days.
When midnight has passed, the goddess,
having arrived and being well-pleased, bestows twenty-five dīnāras daily upon that knower of mantras who desires whatever his heart wishes; of this there is no doubt.
Oṃ oṃ hīṃ Ratipriye svāhā. *Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra*,
Tenth Chapter.
Therein is the ritual for the servant (*ceṭaka*).
Now, the servants are described:
with a mind overcome by passion, one should constantly recite the mantra at night.
This mantra, when recited, necessarily brings about subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter.

Oṃ aiṃ skīṃ klīṃ klīṃ sahavallari klīṃ kāmapiśāca klīṃ hrīṃ kāmapiśāca, I desire such-and-such a passionate woman; seize her with passion! 2 Tear her with your nails in my dream-form! 2 Make her melt! 2.
"Bind, bind with the weapon-mantra! Śrīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!
For three months, Kambala, his mind perfectly serene, should recite this mantra;
he shall then perform the raising of the dead and likewise cause an image to move. (UT 10.2)

"O Mahādevadūta clad in a perpetually red blanket, raise up the corpse! Raise it up! Move the image! Move it! Shake the mountains! Shake them! Play with ease! Play with ease! *īṃ īṃ phaṭ svāhā!* One who is pure should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times on the shore of the ocean;
he will certainly effect the summoning of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth. (UT 10.3)
One who performs the rite of summoning by means of the *abhaya-ghudghutā* should recite this mantra—beginning with "O son of creation, summon so-and-so!
*drīṃ*!"—eight thousand times over the course of seven days.
Daily, the one named Maṇibhadra bestows a single silver coin.
Oṃ, homage to Maṇibhadra; homage to Pūrṇabhadra; homage to the great yakṣa, the lord of armies, who bears the *mauddha-mauddha*, the bearer of the well-fashioned seal, svāhā!
One should offer the bali-oblation at the three junctions of the day and recite the mantra at night;
indeed, one should recite it a thousand times daily until a dream arises. (UT 10.5)
It declares the time of death for living beings without a doubt.
*Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya dehi me vacanasiddhividhānaṃ pārvatīpate hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hreṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*.
One should recite this mantra every night on the shore of the ocean, remaining pure.

When one hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the accomplished Sāgaraceṭaka grants [his boon]. At that time, the wise practitioner should maintain silence regarding the Three Jewels; he should always recite the mantra ten thousand times at night so that he may be happy.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with lotuses mixed with honey and milk, using one-tenth of that [number].
The mantra is: *oṃ namo bhagavate rudra dehi me nijarāśiṃ śrīṃ namo 'stu te svāhā / oṃ hrīṃ amukaṃ rañjaya svāhā*.

By means of this mantra, all people become enamored of one; furthermore, by meditating on the night-stalker (*niśācara*) and reciting it with one's own hand, one obtains the lore (*vidyā*) that renders one invisible.
*Oṃ namo rasācāriṇe maheśvarāya mama paryaṭane sarvalokalocanāni bandhaya 2 devi ājñāpayati svāhā*.
By merely uttering it once, the mantra known as the *nṛsiṃhaceṭaka* destroys the afflictions of *ḍākinīs* and other such beings.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the shatterer of the strength of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who pervades the three worlds; to the uprooter of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, *yoginīs*, and *ḍākinīs*;
to the one arisen from the pillar: destroy, destroy all faults! Disperse, disperse! Shake, shake! Grind, grind! Hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā!
Come, come, O Rudra, the Lord commands it: svāhā!
The impeller, thousand-footed, draws forth sleeplessness:
Oṃ, O Impeller, cause [the woman] so-and-so to enter your maṇḍala; liquefy her, burn her, torment her! HAUṂ. (Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra 10.9)
The Eleventh Chapter:
Now, the mantra for the binding of the directions:
*Vajrakrodhāya mahādantāya daśadiśo bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Now, regarding the contraction of the vagina:
having ground *kumuda* and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), one should smear it upon the vagina;
after three nights or five nights, the vagina becomes contracted. (UT 11.1)
Māṃsī, sandalwood, mustā, tagara, and nāgakesara—
with these, an application for a month and an ointment for the vulva is supreme.
With *mālatī* flowers, oils, and bark, an ointment for the private parts [is prepared].
Or, if she should do so during her fertile period, then she will become equal to him.
Having brought the five parts of a *ḍimba* tree and cooked them in mustard oil, by constantly applying this as an ointment, she shall bring her husband under her control.

One should smear the root of the *vānarī* plant with goat’s urine; by that application, one may then forcefully enjoy the penis as one desires. Saubhāgyapippalī, lac, and poison, increased in sequence [by one part each],...
A woman desires a man for a long time after his body has been smeared with this ointment and washed.
Likewise, the application of pigeon, guñjā, white lotus,
and honey to the navel is said to be a supreme means for arresting semen.
One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel provided with saffron on birch bark,
or on cloth, or on an eye-ointment, a bound fruit, or the like.
On each individual petal, one should write the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, which is supremely radiant.
Likewise, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be placed specifically in the center of the pericarp;
with that primary mantra encased [in the *vidarbha* fashion],
one should fashion a firm image within the circle using all types of clay.
One will undoubtedly attract even proud women;
they do not return to a state of detachment but remain in the condition of a servant.
