[The recipe consists of] pomegranate, pañcakola, iron, vajrīrasa, and ghee.
A powder made from bhūmandara, śākhā, teeth, and nails indeed brings [others] under one's control.
Manahśilā, priyaṅgu, rocanā, and nāgakesara,
when combined with collyrium for the eyes, bring all sentient beings under control.
Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra, Twelfth Chapter:
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ draṃ, O fierce and terrible one, O three-eyed one, O Cāmuṇḍā, O destroyer of misfortune! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
"Hrīṃ! I bow to Mahādeva, Nṛsiṃha of terrifying form; Oṃ, salutations to Him!
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"In [the place] filled with Uḍḍīśa and crowded with hosts of yogins..."
Having bowed her head, Gaurī questioned Śaṅkara. The Lord said:
"Listen, O lady of beautiful hips, for the sake of your daily success."
I shall tell you all of that, O Goddess, which has been gathered together for you.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that a twice-born man who would strike back with mantras against another brahmin—
out of devotion to you, I shall describe to you the Uḍḍīśa previously mentioned by me.
Having paid homage to Uḍḍīśa and to Rudra, who is indeed very difficult to conquer—
the one with matted hair, the odd-eyed one, who brings fear to all beings—
[there is] first the "creation of beings" (bhūtakaraṇa) and likewise second, the "intoxication" (unmādana).
The third is indeed subduing through hatred, and the fourth is likewise eradication;
the fifth is the eradication of a village, the sixth is the stopping of water,
the seventh is the stopping of fire, and the eighth is the power of subjugation.
Listen also, O fair-faced one, to other excellent applications:
the yogas taught by Śiva in the *Uḍḍīśa*, the definitive scripture,
[such as] blinding, binding, and likewise making mute.
Likewise, the contraction of limbs and causing fever in living beings;
the breaking of missiles and weapons, the destruction of water,
the consumption of curd and honey, and similarly, the scratching with the nails.
There will certainly be mutual provocation between elephants and horses,
the dragging of serpents, and likewise among men;
there will be the destruction of crops and the cause of miscarriage of fetuses.
There is the accomplishment of the *vetāla* and *añjana*, as well as the accomplishment of the owl;
now hear also of other extremely fierce applications,
including the employment of spells and mantras, and the medicinal herbs used for malevolent rites.
They must be kept secret, made even more secret, and guarded with great effort from one who is of low birth,
of inferior intellect, devoid of devotion,
as well as from the harmful, the base, and especially the slanderous.

Those men who, greedy for fruits and other gains for their own sake, do not respect the instruction [of the teacher]— under this curse, they must be avoided with great effort. Wise men should never form an association with such people.
Those deluded ones who create divisions within the power of the ritual of Uḍḍīśa are wicked and indeed difficult to overcome; what is the use of speaking much more on this?
If one desires the accomplishment of one's own will for the sake of oneself, [then one should follow this].
It should be given to a virtuous person who is devoted to the gods and the guru.
However, practitioners should employ these applications when there is a cause for an enemy;
they cease without further motive once one's own self is grasped—of this there is no doubt.

For one who is dissatisfied and undisciplined should not practice these applications; however, the investigations established by the scriptures, which are the proximate causes [of success], are auspicious. Oṃ glauṃ gaṃ, homage to Gaṇeśa.
With this mantra, the knower of mantras should fashion an image of Lambodara from potter’s clay and worship it with ritual offerings.
This should be recited attentively during the three junctions of the day for seven days.
Through recitation one thousand times, peace shall arise.
By reciting eight more than that (eighteen) in the morning, a person shall obtain auspicious intelligence;
and within one month, O Mistress of Gods, the attainment of prosperity will certainly occur.
O lady of excellent hips, within six months one shall become a great lord of wealth,
and within one year one shall undoubtedly become a knower of the knowledge of the three times.
Aiṃ namaḥ svāhā.
In the morning, one should worship the Great Goddess Varadā by reciting [the mantra] one thousand times, using white perfumes and ointments,
flowers, japa, and daily offerings such as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).

Indeed, on the very seventh day, such mastery of speech arises; one becomes an immediate expounder and a bearer of the Śruti and Smṛti. As a kinsman to all beings, one prospers with long life and happiness.
O Goddess of the gods, with this mantra *oṃ klīṃ*, the practitioner should begin the recitation (*japa*).
Constantly clothed in red garments and likewise smeared with saffron paste on his limbs, he shall,
by merely reciting for seven days, bring even the women of the gods under his control.
Oṃ drīṃ drīṃ drīṃ drīṃ svāhā!
One who has previously performed the ritual should recite this while staying in solitude;
it is praised for summoning a woman who is excellent, well-adorned, and beautifully dressed.
Oṃ haiṃ haḥ huṃ.
O Dear One, by employing the upward gaze, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
thus, liberated from all sins, one is born in the state of a sky-farer (khecara).
Oṃ drīṃ kārīṇḍaḥ kṣaḥ kṣīṃ phaṭ svāhā. Standing on one foot, O auspicious lady, one should recite this one hundred and eight times.
Whatever object one desires, that it bestows day after day.
And one should worship that distinguished man with offerings to the gods, the fire, the guru, and the brahmins.
With this mantra: *oṃ śrīṃ kṣīṃ lohaṃ muñca kili kili amukaṃ kāṭaya kāṭaya mātaṅgini svāhā*, worshipping with ritual services in the forenoon, [one should perform the rite].
Having filled a shallow bowl with food, one should offer it as a *bali* at a crossroads.
If a man casts this with the mantra and sees another person, he will certainly accomplish his intended tasks; it cannot be otherwise.

"Oṃ stambhini svāhā, kapālini svāhā, drīṃ drīṃ vaiṣādārthini svāhā, chaḥ chaḥ. Having consecrated the clay with this mantra, having enchanted it seven times in water, and having brought [the deity] face-to-face, one should cast it [into the water] and recite the mantra ten thousand times during the day. (UT 12.34)
By this, the mantra of the practitioner will undoubtedly become perfected.
Oṃ śrīṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ.
At the time of midday, one should perform the recitation facing the sun.
By merely reciting it ten thousand times, one perceives one's own power;
by the mere falling of one's gaze, bipeds and quadrupeds become overcome by fever, through the unprecedented perfection of the mantra.
Oṃ haṃsaḥ haṃsaṃ so 'haṃ svāhā. By means of water over which this has been recited twenty-one times, one afflicted by fever is liberated merely by drinking it; he immediately becomes healthy.
Oṃ drīṃ! Homage to Ghorēśvarī, Ghoramukhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Ūrdhvakeśī, Vikṛtānanā! Drīṃ drīṃ hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ svāhā!
This is the mantra for the crushing of all [obstacles].
Oṃ drīṃ drīṃ drīṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! By the striking of fingers, cause the terrifying of all seizing spirits (grahas)!

Oṃ sraṃ srāṃ sriṃ srīṃ sruṃ srūṃ sreṃ sraiṃ sroṃ srauṃ sraṃ sraḥ ha raṃ rauṃ rīṃ rūṃ raiṃ reviḥ chuṃ chuṃ haṃsaḥ amṛtavarcase svāhā. Having condensed water into a shallow bowl with this mantra and consecrated it one hundred and eight times, one should drink it upon rising in the morning. Within a year, one becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair. Furthermore, by assuming the form of trees, stationary objects, or moving beings, and by the acceptance of [their] limbs, one reduces to ashes the tiger’s fur and so forth previously consumed by hunger; one becomes beloved by all people and attains a long life.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to Rudra, the Lord Caṇḍeśvara, huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
By performing recitation with this mantra, one shall swiftly obtain what is desired.
Oṃ hūṃ drīṃ kṣaṃ kṣāṃ kṣiṃ kṣīṃ kṣuṃ kṣūṃ kṣeṃ kṣaiṃ kṣoṃ kṣauṃ kṣaṃ kṣaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
One should first recite this mantra one hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand oblations as its tenth part.

One should offer each fuel-stick smeared with clarified butter; thus it becomes perfected. In the world of Gaṅgāgoloka, no clouds perish, nor does Vāsava send rain; he dries up rivers and oceans, and there occurs a paralyzing of the clouds.
Standing in the midst of water, one performs recitation; during a time of drought, it causes heavy rain. *Oṃ drīṃ pracalite kubere hūṃ hūṃ kili kili svāhā*.

During the first watch of the night, near a mirror-lamp, one causes the Youth (Kumāra) to enter a vessel six finger-breadths wide containing a solar disc on its left side. First, ten thousand recitations must be performed, and worship with the five offerings must also be performed.
And previously, in one's own kingdom:
*Oṃ śrīṃ himajāte prayaccha me dhanaṃ svāhā*. With this mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight white mustard seeds mixed with ghee, combined with food and drink.

If one performs a thousand oblations, one shall obtain what is desired by the mind; if ten thousand, one shall become possessed of beautiful splendor; if a hundred thousand, one shall obtain a hundred villages. Oṃ namo namaḥ.
One should recite this mantra one hundred times; this mantra bestows all desires.
*Oṃ drīṃ śrīṃ sārase siddhikari krīṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times and worship constantly with red oleanders (*karavīra*); this mantra bestows all desires.

Oṃ druṃ kṣeṃ kṣeṃ huṃ kṣaḥ [name] kṣaḥ svāhā! By means of this mantra, one should offer into the fire *rājikā* (black mustard), salt, husks, thorns, and the remains of offerings to Śiva, mixed with oil; one will thereby become a vessel for all prosperity. Oṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ lūṃ laṃ lauṃ huṃ laḥ [name] chaḥ chaḥ svāhā!

With this mantra, white mustard seeds should be consecrated together with ashes; by casting them into the house of someone and scattering them with the mantra, the offering-powder, and the dust, that person’s arms will become paralyzed.

If one casts them before an enemy army, the enemy host will be paralyzed: the horses, elephants, and men will become motionless, incapacitated, and utterly agitated on all sides. Oṃ ruṃ ruṃ mukhe svāhā.

By washing the face with oil consecrated by this mantra, or by performing an anointing of the limbs with sesame oil, ailments such as wind-disorders (*vāta*) and others are destroyed within seven days.
*Aiṃ mātaṅgi vimalāvati vikarāle drīṃ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā*.
Having consecrated *japā* flowers with this mantra, one should offer them into the water of a river or similar body; within seven days, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
There was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms;
by the mere chanting of his name, what has been taken away or lost is recovered.
One should constantly, constantly recite some mantra for the sake of obtaining wealth.
Oṃ maṃ kiṇi svāhā. This is the mantra for scorpions. Oṃ huṃ huṃ haṃsaḥ haṃsaṃ so 'haṃ so 'haṃ svāhā.
Thus ends the mantra for removing all poisons.
One should perform the cleansing of that body with a peacock feather, *kuśa* grass, an arrow, or an arrow-shaft, while reciting:
*haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ huṃ hūṃ heṃ haiṃ hoṃ hauṃ haṃ haḥ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā*.

One should contemplate this [syllable], which resembles cow’s milk, again and again upon the face of the one with the beautiful countenance, then on the head, the body, then the throat, then the heart, the navel-center, the secret place, and likewise on all the limbs; thus, O lady of excellent hips, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), even one bitten in the throat lives. OṂ GAṂ GAṆAPATAYE MAHĀGAṆAPATAYE VIGHNAHARĀYA MATAṄGASAMBHAVĀYA LAMBADARĀYA GAURĪPRIYAPUTRĀYA HRĪṂ GĀṂ NAMAḤ RAṂ HAṂ KṢAḤ SVĀHĀ.

One should draw the figures marked with *gorocanā*, poison, mustard seeds, long pepper, *nīca* grass, barley, and *mahātaila*, along with the *devadatta* [mantras]; having offered oblations into a fire made of *nimba* wood, one should draw them on the back [of the effigy], whereby fever is immediately destroyed and peace is attained.
(Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra 12.46)
The Thirteenth Chapter. Oṃ drīṃ vidyāstambhini stambhini chaḥ chaḥ svāhā!
One should first recite this mantra ten thousand times (ayuta), and thereafter one should contemplate it with the mind.
One obtains food even in the middle of the forest.
*Oṃ hauṃ namo bhagavate mahārudrāya uḍḍāmareśvarāya huṃ huṃ chaṃ chaṃ drīṃ drīṃ svāhā*.
With this mantra, for the purpose of consecration, one should have a flask prepared over which it has been recited one thousand times; within that [flask], one should place the five jewels.

Having placed [the vessel] and wrapped it with a white cloth, one should take that jar— which contains a well-ground mixture of various fruits and is adorned with various gems— and reside within its gateway-like chamber; then, at night, together with a woman, one should go to a cremation ground, a forest tree, a solitary tree, the bank of a river, a river flowing to the ocean,
or a crossroads.

Then, having taken the jar, a woman who is barren, or one whose children have died, or one who is unfortunate, or one who has given birth only once, or one who is broken—any such woman becomes beloved by all people; she should rub herself with [the following]:

priyaṅgu, saffron, gorocanā, nāgakesara, dūrvā, the two types of haridrā, the two types of siddhārthaka, vacā, punarnavā, apāmārga, arka, citraka, śālmalī, lakṣmaṇā, tālamūlī, śatāvarī, vandhyākarkaṭī.
Balā, kṣīriṇī, mṛgapippalī, likewise cirāṇi, supattrāṇi, uśīra, ghee, honey, as well as the flowers and leaves of palāśa,
the leaves of ambara and bilva, aśvagandhā and other fragrant substances— all these, according to the specific requirements of the rite,
one should use to rub the body; furthermore, whatever is used as an ointment for the head, having placed it in a jar, one should bathe with it and obtain a wife.
Always, having discarded her own garment for rubbing the body, she should put on another's garment.

Seated upon an auspicious seat, she should perform the rite; having poured water contained in a jar, she who draws in the machine (*yantra*) in the midst of women should then honor the woman standing face-to-face with her.
With garments, ornaments, vermilion, fragrant flowers, and other such items, one should perform the worship of the deity in the home; one should worship Lord Śiva together with the Goddess.
That man should give a sacrificial fee consisting of a white cow accompanied by its calf.
Now I shall declare the fruit of bathing as it was spoken by Tripurāri:
one desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains wealth;
one desiring peace attains peace; and the unfortunate becomes fortunate.
Likewise, a king who has lost his kingdom will certainly regain his kingdom;
one without a wife shall obtain a wife, and one seeking happiness shall attain happiness.
Thus ends the fruit of bathing for women and men.
*Huṃ amukaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā.* Having gone to a cremation ground, one should very quickly take the milk of an owl, a pigeon, and a *kāñjīra*, and recite [this mantra] for seven days.

*Huṃ amukaṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.* Standing near a *bhānu* tree, one should recite this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*). Then, one should perform a fire offering (*havana*) with mustard oil in a tenth part of that amount; this results in the power of causing [an enemy] to fall down.
Having first recited the mantra *oṃ oṃ oṃ* ten thousand times (*ayuta*), if one recites it during a time of drought, a great rain will fall.

Having first recited the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ varade svāhā* ten thousand times, one should perform a fire-oblation (*havana*) with a tenth part of that number using *palāśa* wood fuel-sticks and offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Thereafter, one shall obtain results at all times.
*Huṃ huṃ huṃ naṃ naṃ naṃ amukaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), one should smear fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood with blood and offer them as oblations (*hunet*) one-tenth that number while uttering the name of the person [targeted].
By a single thousand such offerings, that person is seized by a great fever of Indra; likewise, by ten thousand offerings, they are brought down by this very same method.
One should offer ten thousand oblations of Apāmārga wood fuel sticks mixed with the three sweets while reciting the mantra; thereafter, Vibhīṣaṇa and the other Rākṣasas become granters of boons.
Oṃ hūṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaṃ vaḥ oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the mantra for seizing fever:
Oṃ aiṃ kṣili kili phaṭ svāhā.

Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times over an udumbara fruit mixed with the three sweets, one should perform a fire oblation (homa) of one thousand; this brings about a great rain during a time of drought.
Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ draiṃ drauṃ haḥ oṃ svāhā!
Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of *bilva* wood fuel smeared with the three sweets; thereafter, all people of the realm become one's servants.
Oṃ drīṃ oṃ drīṃ huṃ oṃ svāhā!

Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), one should offer oblations of *darbha* fuel-sticks mixed with ghee and milk for one-tenth that number; through ten thousand such homas, all diseases are pacified.

*Oṃ klīṃ amukīṃ khe khe svāhā*. One should first offer this mantra ten thousand times, and then offer *nyagrodha* fuel-sticks mixed with honey for one-tenth that number; by performing merely one thousand homas, the wife of a great king becomes submissive, as do the women of other worlds.
What need is there for further words?
*Oṃ drīṃ gomukhi gomukhi sahasrasutālā bhīmabhogapiśitabhūmau āgacchatu svāhā*!
With this mantra, one who desires subjugation should offer red *karavīra* flowers mixed with honey; one should offer salt to obtain a woman.

One who desires love will attract a previously united partner. One should offer sindūra; there will be an upheaval in the city. One should offer husks and grain-pods; there will be the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra). One should offer human flesh mixed with ghee; one will become a great lord of wealth. Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya uḍḍāmareśvarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
With this mantra, one should offer oblations of ghee mixed with *śrīphala* fruits. By a hundred oblations, wisdom is attained;

by a thousand, the acquisition of cattle; by a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), the gain of a thousand villages; and by one hundred and twenty-five thousand (*sapādalakṣa*), a king who has lost his kingdom regains it.

Oṃ aiṃ drīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā! With this mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations of crow’s flesh and cock’s seed with mustard oil; having recited the name ending in *drīṃ* as many times as there are recitations, the person whose name was thus invoked becomes insane. By offering a thousand oblations of rice, he becomes restored to health. (UT 13.15)
Oṃ aiṃ śrīṃ kṣaṃ klīṃ svāhā.

Recitation (japa) should be performed with this mantra: by reciting it seven times, purification of the body occurs; by reciting it one hundred times, the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrtha) is obtained;
by one thousand times, there is an increase of intelligence; by ten thousand times, one becomes a great poet who composes thousands of works; and by one hundred thousand times—

By two hundred thousand recitations, one becomes a possessor of the Veda; by three hundred thousand, one becomes a knower of all scriptures; by four hundred thousand, one becomes a knower of the past, future, and present; by five hundred thousand, one becomes a lord of the planets; by six hundred thousand, one becomes a knower of the Vedas, Vedāntas, Purāṇas, and the specific Smṛtis; and by seven hundred thousand, one becomes a Vajratantu [endowed with adamantine power] and dries up rivers even among Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the other gods.

If friendship is not established, then one should perform recitation according to the method taught by Vajra. Then, having been consecrated, he becomes equal to a hundred great seers through the power of the vision; he becomes free from affliction through a thousand; furthermore, through ten thousand he becomes a disturber of cities;
with six times that number he agitates the three worlds; with a third of that he agitates the seven netherworlds; and with a fourth...
With the fifth [recitation], one agitates heaven; with the sixth, one agitates the seven worlds ascending upwards; with the seventh, one agitates the three worlds;
with the eighth, one attracts all living beings, both bipeds and quadrupeds; with the ninth, one attracts everything mobile and immobile;
and with ten lakhs, one becomes like Nārada himself, possessing unobstructed movement throughout all the worlds. One may thus perform [these feats].
He becomes capable of undoing or altering [the effects of] others.

Furthermore, by the rite of casting nectar, if a person recites [the mantra] even once and offers an oblation of white karavīra flowers mixed with the three sweets, he becomes beloved by all people; if one offers aśoka flowers with ghee, one becomes free from sorrow.

One who desires to regain a lost kingdom should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *śrīphala* fruits; he shall obtain the lost kingdom. He should offer lotus flowers mixed with clarified butter, or alternatively, water-lily (*kumudinī*) flowers.
One who desires to cause a downfall should offer peacock meat mixed with pungent oil; by this, death occurs through treachery.
One should offer betel nut (*pūgīphala*), pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), and iron powder (*lohacūrṇa*) [into the fire]; thereby eruptions (*visphoṭaka*) will appear over the entire body.
Through an oblation of milk-tree leaves (*kṣīripattra*) and *bilva* leaves, pacification (*śānti*) occurs.
One should offer sesame fuel-sticks (*tilasamidh*) with pungent oil; by that, incitement of enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) occurs.
When an oblation of dhattūra powder mixed with bone powder, pungent oil, and iron filings is offered, the destruction of enemies occurs swiftly.
One should offer human flesh with ghee; then everything desired by the mind is accomplished. (Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra 13.16)
The Fourteenth Chapter:
*klīṃ kāmāture kāmamekhale viṣayiṇi vararati bhagavati amukaṃ me vaśaṃ kuru vaśaṃ kuru klīṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
With this mantra, at the time of eating, one should consume seven morsels that have been consecrated seven times.
On the seventh day, whether it be a woman or a man, they will become submissive and offer up their own wealth.
*Oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. One should recite this mantra at the three junctions of the day; the destruction of enemies will occur.
*klīṃ kāli kāli mahākāli kole kinyā svāhā*.

Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), one should perform one thousand fire-oblations (*homa*) at the time of twilight; thereafter, Kaṅkālī becomes a granter of boons and bestows four pieces of gold every day.
*oṃ drīṃ drīṃ draṃ draiṃ drauṃ draḥ huṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
Having first recited this mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), one should offer only clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire; from this, attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) occurs.
*Oṃ drauṃ drauṃ hīṃ hīṃ huṃ namaḥ svāhā*.
Having recited this mantra according to the previously described procedure for half a month, attraction occurs.
Oṃ haṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hīṃ svāhā. Thus ends the division of the eastern sword. The mantra for reviving all is: Oṃ huṃ drīṃ draṃ drauṃ draḥ huṃ huṃ.
By this mantra, the destruction of all fevers occurs:
*dīṃ haṃ sini svāhā*.
By this mantra, the subjugation of all people is achieved.
Oṃ hīṃ namaḥ hīṃ phaṭ svāhā.
One should recite this mantra ten thousand times while employing the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), remaining seated upon a corpse and not revealing one's heart-intent (*hṛdaya*).
[Having seized her... having made a pill from that [substance] and placed it in the mouth...
One becomes a Vidyādhara.
Oṃ hīṃ huṃ namaḥ.
One should recite this mantra according to the previously prescribed rule; the accomplishment of the magical sandals (pādukāsiddhi) will occur.
Oṃ kṣaṃ kṣaṃ hrīṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. By reciting this mantra according to the previous procedure, the accomplishment of the vetāla is attained. Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā.
Having taken a human skull with this mantra and having placed human oil within it, one should light a wick that increases the eyesight of crows.
On the new moon day of the dark fortnight, on a Saturday, one should cause soot to fall in a blind well, a cremation ground, or an empty shrine,
while reciting the previously mentioned mantra for as long as there is a remainder of the wick.

When it blazes at the conclusion, a profuse offering (bali) must be made there. Taking a sacrificial pillar (balistambha) and having one's eyes anointed with that *siddhāñjana*, one is not seen even by gods or demons; what need is there to mention other people?
Oṃ hraṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ hrīṃ hrīṃ—this is the *Śaṅkhinī* mantra.
Oṃ hīṃ huṃ is the piercing with a handful of flowers; huṃ huṃ is the piercing with the syllable huṃ;
oṃ hrīṃ huṃ is the piercing of the abode.
Hrāṃ is the mantra for piercing with Śivā;
Hrīṃ is the piercing through the friction of the revolving bees;
Oṃ drīṃ huṃ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā.

Having fashioned an iron trident and ground poison with blood, one should smear the trident with it and empower it with ten thousand recitations. Then, burying it in the earth while uttering the name of a person, that person’s death will swiftly occur.
*Oṃ hrīṃkāri hūṃkāri kapāli samāvedhaṃ bandhuṃ napuṃsakaṃ mahāśaye abhayaṃkari amarākhyaṃ kuru kuru jvaraṃ hana hana ākrośāt kolāhalaṃ parāṃ śaktyākarṣiṇīṃ sarvaśaktiprasaṅginīm.*
In rites for pacification: *śāntike huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should mentally recollect this great vidyā that brings enemies under control; he becomes fearless everywhere.
*Oṃ oṃ oṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ sāṃ*. Having recited this mantra, it becomes the destroyer of poisons, both stationary and mobile.
Oṃ asthi yaṃsthi vidrānidrā saṃnividyā rā ṭaṃ ṭīṃ drīṃ samāsaṃ maṭaṃṭīṃ chaṃ chaṃ.
By means of this mantra, one should offer a thousand burnt oblations of crow feathers; he [for whom the rite is performed] by name is expelled.

STRĪṂ HAṂ. When this mantra has been recited ten thousand times, the science of poetry arises. Indeed, if one recites the science of the *strīmaṇi* and the *śakuna*, it instantly produces poetic talent.
HAṂ AIṂ HAṂ HAṂ AIṂ VADA VADA VĀGVĀDINI SVĀHĀ.
By reciting this mantra seven times, it produces ever-increasing poetic skill.
OM HAṂ CHAṂ CHAṂ CHAṂ AIṂ NAMAḤ SVĀHĀ.

This mantra bestows the gift of poetic composition; with more than a thousand recitations, it immediately paralyzes the speech of a speaker upon mere sight. *Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ*—this is the *Vidyā* that paralyzes speech and restores life through the vital breath: *huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ khaṃ khaṃ khaṃ khaṃ chaṃ chaṃ*.
*Drīṃ* is the piercing of light, the piercing of the beyond.
*Hrīṃ* is the mantra for all piercings.
*Draṃ drauṃ drauṃ drauṃ draṃ amukaṃ bheji bheji hrīṃ chaṃ chaṃ chaṃ*: this is the Reviver of the Bursting [of the Veils], which brings success in one's undertakings through its mere observation.
Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ, destroy the eastern rākṣasas, shatter all [obstacles], satisfy [them] and delude them with a great sound! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for slaying all bhūtas.
Oṃ hrīṃ saḥ drāṃ chaḥ chaḥ chaḥ; this is the vidyā that brings about all peace through the homa offering of dūrvā grass and milk.
Huṃ pañcāṇḍaṃ cāṇḍaṃ drīṃ phaṭ svāhā. With this mantra, one should [use] a human-bone kīla seven finger-breadths long.
If one buries [this substance] consecrated a thousand times in someone’s house, a trap that destroys him arises; once it is extracted, he returns to health.
With this mantra—*huṃ kṣaṃ amukaṃ phaṭ svāhā*—one should offer as oblation the flesh of an owl combined with pungent oil; by a thousand oblations, one brings down the enemy. *Uttaratantra 14.19*
Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dhuṃ dhuṃ haṃ haḥ svāhā. This is indeed the vidyā named Trailokyavijayā;
this mantra grants all desires when remembered mentally. UT_14.20
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, O you of universal form, O Piśācinī! Speak, speak the past, future, and so forth; tell me, tell me into my ear! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the full moon, one should recite this mantra one thousand times at the three junctions of the day.
Every day, one should offer purified water, ghee, and a ball of rice on top of a mansion at night. Whatever [power] there is in the three worlds...
Such a discourse speaks into the ear of the practitioner regarding the past, the future, and so forth.
Oṃ raṃ rāṃ saṃ sāṃ laṃ lāṃ haṃ haḥ saṃ saḥ khaṃ khaḥ taṃ taḥ dhaṃ saṃ sphuṃ sphaḥ hrīṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣauṃ sauṃ saḥ chaṃ chaḥ dhaṃ saḥ sphuṃ sphaḥ hrīṃ huṃ.

Hūṃ hūṃ kṣīṃ kṣīṃ kṣauṃ saṃ phaṃ phaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the mantra for destroying all poisons. Oṃ, in the world of the moving and the unmoving; oṃ, in the world of the moving and the unmoving; hūṃ hūṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ haṃ kṣa kṣa kṣaḥ.

Hasaḥ oṃ saṃ huṃ hrīṃ! O Lord of All, by the power of Viṣṇu, by the pride of Śaṅkara, by the speed of Vāyu, by the splendor of Ravi, and by the radiance of Candra—speak the remedy for enmity, for arrows, and for chaff; speak the all-poison-remover! Destroy, destroy all *rākṣasas*! Shatter, shatter them! Delude, delude all the wicked!
O God, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having recited this mantra one thousand and eight times, or a hundred times, on the seventh day success occurs; there is summoning.

*Oṃ hrīṃ [Name] chaḥ chaḥ*. With this mantra, a stake made from human bone eleven finger-breadths long, consecrated with a thousand recitations, should be buried in the house of whomever [one desires]; for that person there will be ruin and destruction. When it is extracted, however, health is restored.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Kāla, Kaṅkāla, Mahākāla, you of terrifying countenance! Seize so-and-so! Pierce him with the trident! 2! Cut him with the sword! 2! Huṃ phaṭ chaḥ chaḥ svāhā!

With this mantra, a stake made of Vibhītaka wood, twenty-one finger-breadths long, consecrated one thousand times, is driven into the door of whichever person's house; that person’s body shall fall instantly.
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ huṃ! [Seize] so-and-so! Chaḥ chaḥ!
With this mantra, a nine-finger-long stake made of *siddhikāṣṭha* wood, consecrated one thousand times, is buried in whose house; that person becomes submissive.

*Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mātaṃgini aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ svāhā*. With this mantra, one should offer as an oblation (*homa*) mustard seeds mixed with salt and ghee while reciting the name of a specific person; that woman or man is brought under control and is also drawn near. UT_14.25
Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ chaḥ chaḥ.
By this mantra, one should empower a wooden stake made of *vāḍava* wood, thirteen finger-breadths long, with a thousand recitations; whoever has it buried in his house becomes blind in both eyes.
Oṃ chaḥ oṃ chaḥ chaḥ.
With this mantra, one should consecrate a ten-finger-long stake made of *bilva* wood a thousand times; if one buries it in someone's house, that person, along with their family, becomes a *preta*.

*Oṃ hrīṃ, give [the maiden] named so-and-so to me, svāhā!* With this mantra, one should consecrate a five-finger-long stake made of *pāṭala* wood a thousand times; if one buries it in a temple under the name of a particular person, that person will quickly obtain a maiden.
In the *Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra*,
the fifteenth chapter:
Having drawn a six-cornered (*ṣaṭkoṇa*) yantra, one should write the mantra "Oṃ Kurukulle svāhā" within that hexagon, starting from the eastern corner.
One should write the two syllables "kuru" in the opposite corner;
one syllable should be written according to the sequence of the previous rotation.

Then, having written this mantra on birch bark and placing it in a portion of the threshold at the door of the house, it expels the house-snake; if placed at the entrance of a hole, that which dwells in the hole is surely destroyed.
A red *karavīra* flower, when smeared with the ashes of mango leaves, becomes white at that very moment; likewise, it becomes a pearl when treated with processed sulfur (*gandhaka*) smoke.
In the world, the flower of the red *karavīra* known as *hayamāra*, when combined with sulfur and a cotton wick, ignites at that very moment.
Similarly, when a smear is made with *ṭaṅkana* and turmeric, it acquires the luster of saffron.
When one throws old, dried cow dung into water, then from it a bubble arises due to its fierce heat;

likewise, when the pale earth touches the surface of the ground, the red Karavīra tree is born. Just as a bee might be placed upon a copper vessel in a figurative sense, so too does a certain attachment of the mind arise through the coloring of betel, yet that fades away, just as the color of turmeric vanishes under the rays of the sun. (UT 15.3)

Oṃ hūṃ sati! It is well known that [this is done] with *kurala* saffron from the sound of a bird; its name is also *kroñca*. Having shown the tongue marked with the syllable *krīṃ*, smeared upon the center of the palm of the left hand, and having again shown it from the palm after applying the ashes of the rising universal stream (*viśvadhārā*), one purifies it through the wondrous movement, conditioned by the milk of a child.
If one places warm milk from cows and other animals in a bronze vessel, maintains it at a very high heat, and adds rice, it becomes milk-rice (*kṣīra*).
By lighting a pouch made of birch bark with sesame oil, one may prepare various kinds of food and eatables just as they are prepared in an iron vessel.
Taking a piece of eggplant (*vārtāka*) and *rañjikā*, one should wrap it with thread, light it, and set it ablaze; when wrapped with that thread, the thread burns away while the eggplant is cooked.

Having written the seven vowels in the first row, and having written the seven groups beginning with *ka* in the row below that, one should write [the remaining letters] in the row below that in the sequence beginning with turmeric (*haridrā*). Through the contraction [of the mind] by joining the vowels and consonants there, and through contact with the squares of the syllables and so forth, it arises. Furthermore, a thief who has established a convention by assigning signs among many people knows even his own gaze within the seven-sevens of vowels and so on.
A thief who takes pleasure in the moment during the course of his operation is recognized when he has dealt with valuable goods.
Having thrown a *dhattūraka* seed somewhere or having eaten it, one then obtains the result of its qualities and so forth; such a person is known as "this thief.
However, petty thieves are those who, upon obtaining an object, give it away.

The syllables of the thief’s name, whether inscribed with the milk of trees such as the *kṣīryarka* and others, or written on the palm of the hand, or even made upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatta*), will— upon being touched and crushed— be given for consumption; furthermore, the unwritten name of the thief, together with the leaf, becomes a clod of earth from the interior of the enemy's house.
When earth mixed with the leaves of the *sādhū* plant is placed in water, it sinks; therefore, having touched [the object], one identifies that person as a thief.
Minute lines written with milk or water become clear when rubbed with charcoal powder.

Furthermore, even a counterfeit letter whose characters are written in reverse becomes a faithful representation upon a mirror or similar surface due to the inversion of the characters, and its application becomes exceedingly firm through this method.

In a vessel made of *nimba* wood that is evenly copper-colored, having ground [the ingredients] for the duration of one *yāma*, let there be equal proportions as follows: of *āmalakī*, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *nimba*, and *khadira*.

By means of the juices of *nīrākhyā* and *rājakaravīra*, according to the method of grinding with all the juices until a collyrium (*kajjala*) is produced, each substance individually shall become a pigment (*masidravya*) within the space of one *yāma*.
The powder of the bark of the *śirīṣa* tree, even without *khadira*, produces the red color of betel.
A coconut fruit, together with its kernel, placed horizontally on the ground, splits into two pieces by a single blow from the mouth against its pericarp.
A small wooden wheel, finely constructed, spins on one leg even without heating.

When the upper foot is applied smeared with the seed-stone of the *guñjā* fruit and rendered motionless, then [the person] wanders about to the very tips of the toes; at that time, something shaped like a palm-print attached to the sole of the foot rises up.

Likewise, a puppet made of light wood, provided with a mouth-cover for the purpose of making the wicked laugh, remains standing when it is attached to the waist by means of a white cloth or similar material.
Similarly, charcoal placed in an inverted bronze vessel beneath a tightly covered garment, such as a *jambū* tree branch, does not burn the cloth.

A jar impregnated with the powder of *ānataphala* burns even water mixed with ice; and a sharp [substance] placed in a bell-metal vessel does not become heavy even when boiled. That which was sour then becomes bitter, and that which was sweet becomes sour. Even for the purpose of writing within a book by means of soot and the powder of *cavikā*, it cooks as desired, just as in a most delightful cauldron.

When honey is poured into a vessel such as a fire-pot that has been ignited by fire and is filled with water, [the flame] descends face-downward; it spontaneously emerges through two wicks accompanied by smoke.

Even when the interior of the two wicks is filled with rabbit dung, and the lower wick is positioned below by means of tortoises, the flame of the upper wick—blazing with a crest of sharp embers—also emits blazing smoke through a tube or similar aperture.
This application should be performed in a favorable wind.
When the thread-mark, concealed up to the fingers of the left hand, appears as if markless to a person observing with unevenly spaced eyes, one should know that even an uneven man is [favorable].
One should recognize the number of pills to be equal to the product of the five pomegranates multiplied by the peaks.
When *vakrā* is not in season, by mixing it with the powder of its fruit and ashes along with clarified butter, *kākañjikā* is suddenly produced.
In deep, still water, when writing or thinking is performed with the powder of *dhūmaka*, it speaks like one who is afraid but does not sink;
for half the duration of the immersion in clarified butter mixed with equal parts of *samadaśa* and *ghṛtaja*, the pestle remains suspended in the clarified butter.

Under the Puṣya asterism, even a child can pierce a target, however distant, with an arrow made from saffron. A heap of cow dung is seen to be burning in the center, appearing like blood from a slain hare, by the light of a lamp wick; yet there is no oil at all there. When a cotton wick the size of a mustard seed is made from the fruit of the white Arka plant and combined with oil, then in the flame of that lamp, all the wood of the house—such as the rafters and so forth—is seen as if it were a serpent.
Having placed a serpent in a vessel with holes filled with snake-oil, [the vessel] is situated inside another vessel that is without holes; by applying fire, the water ignites.

At that very moment, the oil—prepared according to the previous method on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and marked with frog-oil—becomes entirely hostile. Having ignited it with the light of a lamp, whatever is seized is characterized by a stalk fashioned from the wings and beak of a cock.
When the letter arrives, one should take a skull of a monkey and fill it with water; at that moment, the jar becomes empty.

Likewise, having smeared the sole of the left foot with a powder of black pepper, ginger, and long pepper—or both combined—one strikes a tree with it, and even a *kalpavṛkṣa* tree produces the fruit of the *nameru*.

Just as a black cow at the time of calving gives birth to a fetus of the same color, so too, when one sees the fruit of the *prajāreṇḍalā* plant grasped in the fist within intense darkness, it will generally yield the fruit; likewise, the *kālāyita-mudrikā*, which resembles the udder of an excellent cow, when fallen upon, grasped, and deposited, produces the eight aforementioned fruits.

If one prepares an ointment from *samuṣṭā*, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) mixed with butter and other substances, and then smears one's hand with it after applying peacock droppings, even Brahmā will not see any object situated there.
If the powder of *phala* is mixed with bathing water and thrown in, it appears as if there were thousands of worms.
By using the dried powder of *hayakālīyaka* together with a cow-head-shaped scrubber (*gavaśīrṣaka*) for an immediate bath in fine water, agriculture with seeds flourishes.
By means of a lower cloth (*adhaḥpaṭa*), having seen the inevitable [result] such as the destruction of crops, one sees the object situated at the tips of the feet.

With the body smeared with hibiscus flowers (*japākusuma*), on a knife or similar tool, a single insect called *kaṇācita* placed within a fruit is congealed like blood. A wick made of cloth soaked in oil and infused with the bark of a milky tree (*kṣīrivṛkṣa*) burns when [the wick] is moistened with water while under a mechanical constraint.
In this way, even a wick combined with sea-oil will burn.
By placing small flowers such as *droṇaka* and others upon the tip of a powder, *dhattūra* seeds sprinkled with water will bear fruit as if they were alive.
Sugarcane, by means of the powder of *kukkuṭī* seeds, is produced instantly like a *sudarśana* leaf.
By placing a smooth cloth upon a stainless bronze vessel facing the sun, fire emerges through the application of a circular shape.
